title: Sphera AI Introduces Agentic AI Supply Chain Risk Tools
content:
Sphera AI Introduces Agentic AI Supply Chain Risk Tools
Prioritise Us
on Google
Sphera has launched new AI capabilities for Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM). Credit: Getty
Sphera CEO Paul Marushka outlines AI-powered supply chain risk management for faster supplier, product and operations decisions
Sphera has launched new AI capabilities for Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM), designed to connect external risk signals with the suppliers, products and operations they could affect.
The new capabilities include agentic AI tools, conversational AI features and a Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows organisations to pull insights directly from SCRM into compatible AI tools.
The Chicago-based company said the technology is intended to help organisations assess disruption impacts and coordinate responses in minutes rather than days. The Agentic AI functionality is built into the existing Risk Response and Resolution product and is available in the existing subscription.
The announcement follows the publication of Sphera research showing that external events - including supplier failures, port closures, material shortages and trade restrictions - are a major source of operational disruption.
Paul Marushka, CEO at Sphera
External risk is becoming operational risk
Across the US, UK, Germany, France and UAE, 58% of surveyed chief operating officers said their most significant disruptions originated at least as much outside their organisation as within it. The figure rose to 71% among respondents in the UAE.
The research surveyed 750 COOs. It found that the most difficult parts of disruption management were:
Identifying exposed suppliers or products: 33%
Selecting the right mitigation action: 30%
Quantifying potential business impact: 29%
The findings reflect a growing gap between risk detection and operational decision-making. Organisations may identify an external event quickly, but still struggle to determine which sites, products, suppliers or customer commitments are exposed.
“The boundary of the enterprise is no longer the boundary of operational risk. A disruption can begin with a supplier, a critical material or an event on the other side of the world, but its consequences are felt inside the business,” says Paul Marushka, CEO and President of Sphera.
"The challenge is connecting those external signals to the products and operations they affect quickly enough to make a better decision. Sphera AI helps close that gap, while keeping people in control of the decisions that matter most,” adds Paul.
"Risk intelligence only matters if it reaches the person making the decision. We produce it once and deliver it where decisions are made, in our interface or headless, inside the AI tools, procurement platforms and data platforms each decision-maker already uses," Scott Lehmann, Group Vice President Of Product Management at Sphera.
Global trade is now leverage. Export controls, tariffs and disruptions like Hormuz expose upstream dependencies that sit several tiers below the suppliers most teams watch.
Scott Lehmann, Group Vice President Of Product Management at Sphera
Sphera notes 58% of surveyed chief operating officers said their most significant disruptions originated at least as much outside their organisation as within it. Credit: Sphera
Sphera AI connects signals to business impact
The new Sphera AI capabilities are designed to link external intelligence to internal business context.
Users can ask questions about supplier and supply chain risk in plain language and identify which suppliers, products and operations may be exposed. The aim is to reduce the need to compare multiple dashboards or manually trace relationships between an external event and the business processes it threatens.
The capabilities include: external risk signals, supplier exposure, product dependencies, operational impact, risk severity, mitigation decisions, response coordination, supply continuity, production protection and revenue protection.
Sphera’s Supply Chain Risk Management platform combines external risk intelligence with suppliers, products, commodities and multi-tier dependencies.
Model Context Protocol extends risk intelligence
Sphera has also added support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
MCP allows organisations to make selected SCRM insights available through compatible artificial intelligence tools. This means risk information can be accessed in the environments where teams already analyse data and make operational decisions.
The potential applications include querying supplier risk through compatible AI assistants, retrieving risk context without switching between systems, connecting external events to internal supplier records, supporting procurement and operations workflows, making trusted risk data available to authorised users and reducing time spent searching across separate applications.
The approach is intended to make risk intelligence more accessible while retaining organisational controls over data, workflows and decision-making.
AI agents support risk triage
Within Sphera’s Risk Response & Resolution Center, the recently introduced AI agents assess risk severity and supplier impact.
The system is designed to help teams distinguish urgent risks from lower-priority signals. By automating aspects of triage, Sphera said users can focus on the events most likely to affect production, supply continuity or revenue.
The Risk Response & Resolution Center provides a central workspace for triaging risks, assigning ownership, executing mitigation plans and tracking outcomes with an audit trail.
Sphera’s broader platform monitors more than 300,000 news sources each day and processes approximately 15 billion data points each month, according to company information.
Human control remains central
Sphera’s announcement positions artificial intelligence as a decision-support capability rather than an autonomous replacement for supply chain and procurement teams.
The company said every one of the 750 COOs surveyed identified at least one risk-management activity they would allow AI to progress automatically, provided appropriate rules and controls were in place.
This creates a governance model in which AI could detect relevant events, classify risk signals, summarise complex information, match events to suppliers, estimate potential exposure, prioritise response activity as well as potentially recommending next steps.
Human teams remain responsible for decisions involving suppliers, production, customer commitments, financial exposure and operational continuity.
Traditional supply chain risk management often stops at the alert. Sphera’s announcement focuses on the next stage: translating an alert into an operational response.
The workflows that follow the identification of such a disruption include: detecting a geopolitical, environmental or logistics event, identifying affected suppliers and sub-tier relationships, mapping impacted products and facilities and estimating operational and commercial consequences. These steps are then followed by the assignment of response ownership, the selection and execution of mitigation actions, and tracking whether an organisation's exposure has reduced.
Sphera describes this connection between risk signals, business impact and response workflows as a way to reduce decision latency across the disruption lifecycle.
Key disruption workflow activities
Detecting a geopolitical, environmental or logistics event
Identifying affected suppliers and sub-tier relationships
Mapping impacted products and facilities
Estimating operational and commercial consequences
Assigning response ownership
Selecting and executing mitigation actions
Tracking whether exposure has reduced

title: GAC launches battery production in Thailand - electrive.com
content:
Inpow Battery Technology, the battery division of Chinese automaker GAC, has started production at a new plant in Thailand. This expands the group's local manufacturing footprint in Southeast Asia.
Image: Inpow
Inpow Battery Technology officially began production at its new battery plant in Thailand on 29 October. The facility is located east of Bangkok, specifically in Si Racha, Chonburi Province. Inpow is responsible for battery production within the GAC Group. The start of production marks another step in the Chinese conglomerate’s expansion of local supply chains in Southeast Asia.
The plant’s opening coincides with another milestone for Inpow: as the company recently announced, its cumulative global production has now reached 300,000 battery packs. These batteries are already used in a range of electric models from the GAC Aion brand, including the i60, N60 and UT.
With the new site in Thailand, GAC can localise battery production closer to its vehicle manufacturing operations. The new battery plant is likely to play a significant role in the further development of the Southeast Asian market. Local production can shorten transport routes and reduce dependence on supplies from China.
GAC Aion already produces locally
This step builds on GAC’s existing expansion in Thailand. As early as July 2024, GAC Aion
opened its own vehicle plant in the Southeast Asian country
. The location is part of the group’s strategy to use Thailand as a production and distribution base for further markets in the region.
With the additional battery plant, an important part of the value chain is now also being localised. The combination of vehicle and battery production could help GAC strengthen its competitive position against other Chinese manufacturers that are also increasingly investing in Southeast Asia.
Thailand is considered one of the most important automotive hubs in Southeast Asia and has been working for several years to align its industry more closely with electric vehicles. The government is promoting the establishment of corresponding production capacities and aims to position the country as a regional hub for electromobility.

title: ExxonMobil on Building a Resilient US Graphite Supply Chain
content:
Materials
Design & Manufacturing
Industry Outlook
Market Analysis
Interviews
ExxonMobil discusses graphite innovation, supply chain resilience, sustainability, and the partnerships needed to successfully scale North America’s battery materials industry.
October 30, 2026
4 Min Read
Venkatesh Vasudevan, Vice President – Graphite Materials at ExxonMobil Product Solutions, at the Battery Show North America.
ExxonMobil
North America’s ambition to build a competitive domestic battery supply chain has put graphite and other critical materials in the spotlight. In this interview,
Battery Technology
speaks with Venkatesh Vasudevan, Vice President – Graphite Materials at ExxonMobil Product Solutions, about the most significant bottlenecks facing North America’s battery materials sector and how the industry can address them.
What are the most significant challenges North America faces in scaling domestic production of graphite and other critical battery materials, and how can the industry address these bottlenecks?
Venkatesh Vasudevan, Vice President – Graphite Materials at ExxonMobil Product Solutions:
North America’s challenge is not simply adding production capacity. It's building capacity that can compete globally in the long run.
Today, many parts of the battery materials ecosystem exist at scale overseas, including infrastructure, supply networks, operating experience, and downstream markets. Building this ecosystem and the associated capabilities in North America will take time, effort, and investment.
Related:
Material Advances Star at The Battery Show
We believe that simply replicating the existing, conventional production model in North America is not the answer. To compete globally, a fundamentally different approach is needed, one that focuses on process innovation and product differentiation. More specifically, for battery anode graphite, we need graphitization technologies that are designed to be more scalable and more energy-efficient than what is used by industry today, and that produce materials superior to what is available today.
And that's exactly where we're focused: applying our technology, engineering, manufacturing, and scale-up capabilities to develop a differentiated approach to standing up graphite supply at scale.
How do you see the evolving requirements from cell manufacturers and OEMs influencing the development and qualification of new battery materials?
Vasudevan:
Customer expectations continue to increase.
Cell manufacturers and OEMs are looking for materials that not only deliver performance, but can also be manufactured consistently, at high quality, and supplied reliably and cost-effectively at scale. There is also a growing desire for anode materials that can work effectively across different battery chemistries, tailored, if you will, to the unique needs of the end-use application, be it grid-scale energy storage, electric vehicles (EVs), or consumer electronics.
That is one reason why we believe early collaboration is critically important. We're working directly with customers throughout the product development lifecycle –understanding requirements, supporting qualification activities, and validating product performance.
Related:
IEA Highlights Growing Demand for Critical Battery Materials
What role do you believe ExxonMobil and other major players in the materials sector should play in fostering partnerships and investments to strengthen the North American battery supply chain?
Vasudevan:
Companies like ExxonMobil can help bring together capabilities that are often difficult to develop independently: end-to-end integration from feed to product, engineering, technology development, manufacturing expertise, project execution, and the ability to deploy capital at scale.
But no one company can build a supply chain alone. Strong collaborations between material suppliers, automakers, cell manufacturers, national labs, academic and research institutions, and policymakers will be essential.
We see our role as helping bridge innovation and commercialization, taking technologies from development through deployment, and ultimately to large-scale manufacturing.
With sustainability becoming a critical factor, how can North America ensure that its battery materials supply chain is not only competitive but also addresses environmental considerations?
Related:
Sabic Launches High-Performance Compounds for EV Power Modules
Vasudevan:
We believe the answer starts with innovation. We're developing an advanced graphitization process designed to improve yield, reduce energy intensity, and lower our manufacturing footprint compared to conventional alternatives.
In fact, our process is designed to deliver up to 50% lower energy intensity than alternative graphitization processes, while also improving throughput and reducing processing times.
Looking ahead to 2030 and beyond, what key innovations or breakthroughs in graphite materials do you anticipate will have the greatest impact on the global battery value chain?
Vasudevan:
The most significant advances will come from combining differentiated graphite materials with more efficient manufacturing processes.
On the product side, we're seeing increasing demand for materials that can enable faster charging, longer cycle life, and higher battery capacity. We are focused on engineering and delivering materials that can significantly improve battery performance.
Independent testing of our advanced graphite against industry alternatives has shown the potential to deliver faster charging and longer cycle life, and more importantly, enable these improvements concurrently. This can help alleviate tradeoffs that industry has had to make between performance and durability.
On the manufacturing side, innovation can drive higher yield, lower energy intensity, and improved scalability. Ultimately, building a competitive North American graphite supply chain will require product and process innovation, and we're focused on both. That's why we believe the opportunity is real, and we can make a meaningful and material contribution.

title: This Week's Top Five Stories in Supply Chain
content:
This Week's Top Five Stories in Supply Chain
Prioritise Us
on Google
Agility Robotics made this week's top five stories. Credit: Agility Robotics
Supply Chain Digital explores the top five stories from the past week, including people moves, robotics deployment and sustainability initiatives
GXO to Deploy Digit 5 Robots in E-Commerce Fulfilment Sites
GXO Logistics is expanding its partnership with Agility Robotics to deploy Digit humanoid robots at two additional US e-commerce fulfilment sites. The deployments are expected to begin in early 2027 at facilities in Statesville, North Carolina, and Lebanon, Tennessee. GXO will initially use Digit 4 units before transitioning to Digit 5 robots when the newer series becomes commercially available.
GXO Logistics has been an early adopter of robotics technology in its logistics operations. The agreement expands on the companies’ multi-year agreement in 2024 to deploy Agility Robotics’ Digit humanoid robots in a live GXO warehouse environment in Flowery Branch, Georgia. Digit units have moved more than 100,000 totes at the Flowery Branch facility, demonstrating the technology’s ability to perform repetitive material-handling tasks reliably in an active logistics environment.
Fabian Köhler, will become Group CEO at Culina Group Limited. Credit: LinkedIn
Culina Announces New CEO After Brand Unification
Culina Group has announced that current Chief Executive Officer Liam McElroy will be succeeded by Fabian Koehler, the Deputy CEO, with effect from 1 February 2027.
The announcement of the executive appointment follows shortly after Culina group announced that it was unifying its subsidiaries under a single brand: Culina.
The announcement in mid October affected established logistics brand names including Culina Logistics, IPS, Stobart, Great Bear, Fowler Welch, Warrens, CML, Stobart Europe, IRF and iForce.
Culina will operate through five specialist divisions: Chilled & Fresh Logistics, Contract Logistics, Transport Logistics, Integrated Packing Services and International Logistics.
WCS & Hershey: Establishing Sustainable Cocoa Supply Chains
The Hershey Company has committed US$2.5m to the Wildlife Conservation Society as part of a four-year project in Cross River State, Nigeria. The partnership aims to
strengthen supply chain resilience
in a region where more than 100,000 households depend on cocoa farming for their livelihoods.
According to the Wildlife Conservation Society, the area contributes almost one third of Nigeria's cocoa exports.
The Cross River State contains Nigeria's largest remaining rainforest and serves as the country's most important cocoa-producing region. This concentration of production makes the region strategically important for maintaining stable cocoa supply chains.
Leidos will deploy AI-driven automation, cloud technology and modern software practices across the Pentagon’s ELMS under a potential US$95m, five-year contract from the DLA. Credit: Getty
Leidos Brings AI to Pentagon Asset Management
Leidos will deploy AI-driven automation, cloud technology and modern software practices across the Pentagon’s Enterprise Logistics Management System (ELMS) under a potential US$95m, five-year contract from the Defense Logistics Agency (DLA).
ELMS is used by more than 50 government agencies to manage over 80 million items of government property valued at more than US$140bn. The system supports asset accountability throughout the property lifecycle and underpins the logistics network that helps keep US warfighters equipped and ready.
The contract extends Leidos’ support for ELMS and its predecessor, the Defense Property Accountability System, to more than 21 years. The agreement includes one base year and four option years, running through August 2031.
ImportGenius offers a source of customs and bill-of-lading information covering more than 25 countries, with data sourced from government customs agencies and other public trade records. Credit: ImportGenius
ImportGenius: AI, Trade Intelligence and Supply Chain Risk
The pressures for supply chain leaders to identify potential supply chain risks, whether those are from
geopolitical
disruption or shifts in the competitiveness of individual suppliers, have never been greater than at present.
Data has become an increasingly important element of competitive advantage. But supply chain leaders understand that the strength of the data they are relying on to identify
disruption
, assess competitors and explain strategic decisions is a key variable.
ImportGenius is a supplier of international trade and supply chain intelligence. Through advanced data management technologies, the firm is able to help its clients make sense of hundreds of millions of shipping manifests and customs records from government agencies and private companies around the world.
Artificial intelligence
can be used to improve trade data quality, support supplier discovery, improve shipment analytics and sharpen supply chain mapping. However, the successful application of AI relies on its use as a support for human decision-making, rather than when it operates without controls.

title: Indian PV at a turning point - pv magazine Global
content: India’s module manufacturing capacity has expanded at remarkable speed, while domestic content requirements are pushing investment into the more complex cell manufacturing sector. Suppliers are also eyeing moves into wafer and ingot manufacturing ahead of further expansion to the domestic content rules. Activity has been more limited in polysilicon manufacturing, as with the development of facilities to produce solar glass and other bill of materials components. The challenge is no longer how much manufacturing capacity India can build, it’s whether that capacity can operate at high utilization, keep pace with fast-changing technologies and compete on cost. “The next phase of expansion needs to be more closely aligned with actual demand, project pipelines and the development of the wider solar value chain,” said Bondada Raghavendra Rao, chairman and managing director at engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) supplier Bondada Group. The scale of the imbalance is becoming increasingly visible. India had built around 233 GW of module manufacturing capacity as of June 2026, against annual domestic demand estimated at 30 GW to 40 GW. Utilization for many of these production lines is running at only 35% to 40%, compared with the 50% to 65% generally considered necessary for sustainable operations. A further 135 GW is planned or under construction. According to Dilip Mehta, director, technical services at project developer Hexa Climate, the issue is not module capacity alone, but its relationship with the rest of the supply chain. He noted that module capacity is currently roughly seven times cell capacity and 116 times ingot and wafer capacity. Adding further module lines widens the gap even further. Capacity pressures Industry executives are divided on whether module additions should slow down, but there is broad agreement that investment decisions need to become more disciplined. Vinay Rustagi, chief business officer at cell and module manufacturer Premier Energies, which recently commissioned one of India’s largest cell manufacturing facilities in Naidupeta, Andhra Pradesh, argues that market forces can automatically correct any imbalance over a period of time. “It is true that more investment is needed on the upstream side of the business. But investment decisions are made based on their individual assessment of demand-supply conditions, pricing and competitive position. There is no need for any government intervention as the market signals automatically correct any imbalance over a period of time,” he said. In practice, sustained overcapacity can put downward pressure on prices and squeeze industry margins, prompting consolidation among those companies best equipped to hang on in these conditions, and encouraging weaker competitors to exit the market. Sourabh Kumar, vice president–strategic investments at module maker and project developer Ampin Energy Transition, says the objective should not be simply maximum capacity, but maximum competitive capacity. He argues that new projects should be assessed on whether the technology is competitive for the next five to seven years, whether the factory can achieve scale and maintain a high utilization rate, whether there is a credible source of raw materials, whether the product can compete with imports on a delivered-cost basis, whether there is sufficient domestic or export demand, and whether the manufacturer has the balance sheet to withstand periods of low margin. “This is particularly important because PV technology is changing rapidly. Investing heavily in a technology that becomes commercially less relevant within a few years can create a bigger problem than having insufficient capacity,” he added. Upstream expansion The Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) – a requirement for all projects backed by India’s government to use components from an approved domestic supplier – has applied to modules since 2021 and was extended to cells in June 2026. The list’s expansion to wafers and ingots is currently set for 2028 and is likely to strengthen the push toward deeper domestic ­manufacturing. But vertical integration will not be practical for every company. Ingot and wafer manufacturing requires significant capital, energy, process expertise and scale. For standalone module manufacturers, Kumar suggests they can remain viable without owning the entire value chain if they build strong supplier relationships, focus on manufacturing efficiency, and differentiate themselves through quality, reliability, product design and customer service. “Vertical integration should not become an objective by itself,” Kumar said. “Integration must improve the economics of the final product, not just increase the number of manufacturing stages under one ownership structure.” Mehta sees cell manufacturing as a more realistic upstream step for standalone module producers than ingots and wafers, given ingot and wafer manufacturing is capital-intensive, power-intensive, and the learning curve is long. Options include backward integration into cells, long-term supply agreements with domestic cell manufacturers, or consolidation with integrated players. The opportunity for upstream investment is clear, but the sequencing will matter. Mehta notes that the ALMM list for wafers will be issued only once at least three independent manufacturing units without common ownership are operational, with a combined annual capacity of at least 15 GW and equivalent ingot capacity. This creates a window for companies to invest in upstream manufacturing, but it also means that first movers carry the risk. Ankit Singhania, director at Gujarat-based cell and module manufacturer Navitas Solar, said the path to integration need not be the same for every manufacturer. Depending on scale and business strategy, companies can explore a combination of organic investments, strategic partnerships, joint ventures and long-term sourcing arrangements with domestic upstream suppliers. “For standalone module manufacturers, integration can also be complemented by investments in automation, quality systems, R&D and next-generation module technologies. Building a competitive ecosystem will require both vertically integrated manufacturers and specialized players with stronger linkages across different stages of the value chain,” adds Singhania. Demand pathways India’s growing solar market provides several potential outlets for excess module capacity. Utility-scale projects remain central, but demand is also emerging from rooftop solar, commercial and industrial installations, open-access projects, and agricultural applications. India’s residential rooftop market could provide an important additional source of demand. The Indian Solar Manufacturers Association estimates annual residential rooftop installations of between 9 GW and 15 GW each year from 2026 to 2030. The PM Surya Ghar scheme, which offers subsidies and concessional financing to rooftop PV customers, is expected to remain a major driver. Floating solar could provide another avenue (see pp.38-41). According to the National Institute of Solar Energy, there is around 102 GW of floating PV potential in India. The government has also approved the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana scheme, targeting 5 GW of floating solar with co-located energy storage. The projects will be sanctioned during fiscal 2026-27 to fiscal 2030-31, with disbursement of financial support continuing up to fiscal 2032-33. Manufacturers also have a significant opportunity to look beyond the domestic market and build a stronger export-oriented business. Singhania says that as countries diversify their clean-energy supply chains, Indian manufacturers are well placed to address emerging demand across BRICS economies as well as other markets in Asia, Africa and the Middle East. This creates an opportunity to utilize manufacturing capacity more effectively while establishing India as a dependable global source for solar modules. Exports, however, are constrained by the higher price of Indian modules compared to those from China. Mehta estimates that Indian module manufacturers can sell comfortably at anywhere between $0.14/W and $0.25/W depending on scale and other factors, compared with about $0.11/W in China, where long-running oversupply has pushed prices even lower than that. That gap narrows only in markets that impose their own restrictions on Chinese supply, so export planning has to be market-specific rather than general. Utilization strategies For manufacturers with idle lines, toll manufacturing or original equipment manufacturer agreements offer another route to utilization. According to Mehta, manufacturers with idle lines can produce for another brand that holds an order book but lacks sufficient capacity. While it does not build brand value, it does convert fixed cost into revenue. Ultimately, utilization itself could become a defining competitive advantage. “A factory operating at 85% to 90% utilization with healthy yields and strong quality can be fundamentally more competitive than a larger factory operating at 30% to 40%,” says Kumar. “This means manufacturers will need to focus much more on demand planning, procurement, inventory management, manufacturing yield, working capital and customer diversification.” India has demonstrated that it can build solar manufacturing capacity at scale. The next test is to create capacity that is competitive, reliable, and technologically relevant. The winners of the next phase may not be those with the largest factories, but those capable of keeping their facilities productive, upgrading them as technology evolves, and finding customers both in India and overseas. title: Farthest human-made object in space loses contact, goes nearly one light-day away from Earth
content: NASA briefly lost contact with Voyager 1 in mid-October after the nearly 50-year-old spacecraft stopped transmitting a detectable radio signal during two scheduled communications attempts. The signal returned on October 20, but engineers are still investigating what caused the interruption. The incident comes just weeks before Voyager 1 is expected to become the first human-made object to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, a point at which radio messages will take a full 24 hours to travel in either direction. NASA’s Deep Space Network, a global system of large radio antennas used to communicate with distant spacecraft, failed to detect Voyager 1’s signal on October 18 and 19. The probe is now approximately 16 billion miles (24 billion kilometers) from Earth. Communication resumed on October 20, about 48 hours after the interruption began. NASA says the team has maintained contact with the spacecraft since then. An automatic safety response may hold the clue Engineers are still trying to determine what triggered the communications loss. However, NASA has established that one group of Voyager 1’s thrusters went offline during the incident, prompting its backup thrusters to switch on automatically. The spacecraft is programmed to respond this way when its onboard computers detect a potential problem with the active thrusters. This automated protection system can place the probe in a stable, safe configuration and pause normal operations while engineers investigate. The spacecraft’s signal returned before the team sent commands to troubleshoot the issue from Earth. “This is the first time we’ve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,” said Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. “We’re relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.” The incident is another reminder of the challenges of operating spacecraft launched nearly half a century ago, especially as their onboard power supplies continue to weaken. NASA is trying to squeeze more life out of Voyager 1 Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, rely on radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs), which convert heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. As the radioactive material decays, the spacecraft lose about four watts of electrical power each year. To keep the probes operating, engineers have gradually switched off instruments and other systems that are no longer essential to their missions. In September, the Voyager team completed a major power-saving effort on Voyager 1, nicknamed the “Big Bang.” Engineers simultaneously switched off three devices and activated lower-power alternatives, helping reduce energy consumption while maintaining the spacecraft’s thermal balance. The procedure was designed to extend the operating life of Voyager 1’s remaining science instruments. Without the changes, NASA estimated that it would have needed to shut down another instrument as early as summer 2027. Both spacecraft are now traveling through interstellar space, beyond the heliosphere, which is the enormous bubble of particles and magnetic fields generated by the Sun. They remain the only spacecraft to have directly studied this region. A 24-hour wait for a message from Earth Voyager 1 is approaching another remarkable milestone . On November 18, 2026, NASA expects the spacecraft to reach a distance of 16.094 billion miles (25.902 billion kilometers) from Earth, equivalent to one light-day. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours. Since radio signals travel at the speed of light, reaching Voyager 1 will then take an entire day. A response from the spacecraft will require another day to return. That means a simple exchange with the probe will take roughly 48 hours, even if everything works as expected. Voyager 1 is currently traveling at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). Launched in September 1977, it has become the most distant human-made object from Earth, having traveled far beyond the planets it was originally sent to explore. The one-light-day milestone will not change the spacecraft’s surroundings or operations. But it will offer a striking measure of how far humanity’s most distant explorer has traveled and how long its signals must journey to reach home.

title: The magnet gap: Building a supply beyond China
content:
Rare-earth permanent magnets are small parts with outsized consequences. A traction motor in an electric vehicle typically carries one to two kilograms of neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB); a direct-drive offshore wind turbine can carry several tons; an F-35 contains an estimated 417 kg of rare-earth material (
CRS R41744
). The magnet sets the torque density of a motor, the size and cooling of a generator, the precision of a servo, and the mass of an actuator. Removing it forces a redesign of the larger machine, and in some applications no equivalent substitute exists. The International Energy Agency estimates that rare earths account for about 40% of the cost of a permanent magnet but under 1% of the value of the car it goes into (
IEA GCMO 2026
). That asymmetry explains the vulnerability that characterizes this supply chain: buyers had little reason to pay for diversification until the parts stopped arriving.
Western governments have moved faster than at any point since the 2010 rare-earth crisis. Washington has taken equity in a miner, guaranteed a price floor, lent hundreds of millions of dollars to magnet start-ups, and launched a strategic stockpile; Europe, Japan, Australia, and Canada have their own programs. Yet announcements, nameplate capacity, and investment commitments are not usable output. A magnet pressed in the United States or Europe may still be made from Chinese-origin metal, sintered in Chinese-designed furnaces, or depend on dysprosium that only China separates at scale.
This report asks a narrower and harder question than whether projects exist. Where does China’s advantage actually reside: in mining, separation, metals, alloys, magnet making, know-how, or the integration of all of them? Which non-Chinese facilities are shipping commercial material now, and how much? How much of the capacity scheduled for 2026 is commissioned, qualified, and reliably delivering? Can producers outside China meet the volume, performance, quality, and cost demands of large buyers? How much can recycling, thrifting and magnet-free motors take off the table? And what would real resilience look like by 2030?
The test applied throughout is simple. The objective is not to count announced capacity but to measure how much reliable, commercially qualified magnet supply can operate without critical Chinese dependencies.

title: Aging warships to get Western eyes to improve naval gun targeting with modern tech
content: The UK’s Chess Dynamics has landed a £3 million ($4 million) contract to supply its SeaEagle fire control system to the Indonesian Navy. Delivered in cooperation with Indonesia’s state-owned PT Len Industri, SeaEagle will be installed on two Bung Tomo -class light corvettes for the Indonesian Navy (TNI AL). These systems will offer the ships greatly improved capability to identify, track, and engage targets (including aerial targets) using their naval guns. To this end, it is not a new offensive capability, but rather an upgrade to existing optics. The SeaEagle Fire Control Electro-Optical (FCEO) is a highly sophisticated, stabilized camera and targeting system. This kind of electro-optical system uses sensors like visible-light cameras and thermal imagers. Depending on the design, such systems can also come with laser rangefinders. Such systems are able to identify and acquire targets like vessels and other objects even in low-light conditions. Giving old seadogs new eyes These maritime surveillance systems are able to track moving objects by keeping their sensors trained on a target despite the ship rolling, pitching, and  changing directions. The system is also able to calculate targeting information like bearing, elevation, and range that can be fed to the ship’s 76 mm OTO Melara guns. Importantly, SeaEagle will interface with the ships’ existing Thales TACTICOS Combat Management System. What’s more, SeaEagle’s cameras can operate passively, meaning they don’t need to transmit detectable signals like radar. This makes the system particularly useful for discreet target tracking, although its laser rangefinder does emit detectable pulses when used. This is very interesting, as using radar can announce its presence. Electro-optical tracking can be considerably more discreet, although lasers are detectable and the system remains limited by visibility and atmospheric conditions. The main advantage of this for the Indonesian Navy is that their ships will effectively be able to upgrade gun capability without replacing the guns wholesale. It will also enable the Indonesian Navy to beef up parts of its roster without commissioning new vessels. The three Bung Tomo -class warships are British-built vessels that Indonesia acquired after their original customer, Brunei, declined to take delivery. Being corvettes, they are relatively small warships, but still capable of carrying out significant naval operations. So, rather than buying entirely new vessels, Indonesia is modernising its electronics, sensors and command systems. According to reports, one, the KRI Usman Harun (359), already has SeaEagle installed. Part of a wider upgrade package The KRI Bung Tomo ( 357) and KRI John Lie (358) will now be upgraded under this new contract. According to reports, this forms part of a larger modernization program for the Indonesian Navy . Other upgrades will include SMART-S Mk2 radar system, STIR EO Mk2 fire controls, and Vigile Mk2 R-ESM designed to detect and analyze electromagnetic signals emitted by other platforms. There is overlap in the capabilities of some of these, but this is by design. They not only complement each other, but also provide a level of redundancy, which is critically important for modern warships . It is worth noting that the modernisation of KRI Usman Harun was originally expected to be completed by the end of 2023. However, the work has taken considerably longer than anticipated, highlighting the potential complexity of integrating modern systems into ageing warships

title: Why can’t data centers simply move to the Arctic or beneath the ocean?
content: Data centers have a rather inconvenient habit of getting hot. Thousands of processors crunching through calculations, training AI models, and storing the world’s digital information generate enormous amounts of heat. Keeping all that hardware from overheating takes substantial amounts of electricity, making cooling one of the industry’s biggest engineering challenges. So, why not put these facilities somewhere naturally cold? The Arctic has plenty of freezing air, while the ocean offers a vast reservoir of relatively cool water. Better still, why not put servers directly underwater and let the sea do the cooling? It sounds like an obvious solution. And engineers have explored both ideas. But building a data center is about considerably more than keeping its servers chilly. The Arctic has a cooling advantage Data centers in cold climates can use a technique known as free cooling. Instead of relying entirely on energy-intensive chillers and refrigeration systems, facilities can use cold outside air or water to remove heat from their equipment. This can significantly reduce the electricity needed for cooling. It is one reason companies have established data center operations in places such as Sweden, Finland, Iceland, and Norway. Google’s facility in Hamina, Finland, for example, uses seawater from the Gulf of Finland as part of its cooling system. But there is a difference between building in a cold country and building in the Arctic wilderness. The farther north a facility goes, the harder it can be to access reliable electricity, high-capacity fiber-optic networks, skilled workers, and transport infrastructure. A data center may need less energy to cool its servers, but it still needs enormous amounts of electricity to run them. That is becoming an increasingly important constraint. The International Energy Agency has highlighted the growing electricity demands of data centers, while grid connection delays and limited power infrastructure are becoming major obstacles to expansion. In other words, finding a cold patch of land is easy compared with finding one that can reliably power a massive computing facility. There is also the matter of getting there. Construction materials, replacement servers, and maintenance crews have to travel through regions where harsh weather, long distances, and limited transport links can complicate even routine operations. Permafrost and changing Arctic conditions introduce further engineering challenges for buildings and infrastructure. What about putting data centers underwater? The ocean offers another tempting proposition. Submerge a sealed facility, circulate heat into the surrounding water, and potentially reduce the need for conventional cooling equipment. Microsoft actually tested this idea through Project Natick. In 2018, the company deployed a sealed data center module off the coast of Scotland’s Orkney Islands. Roughly the size of a shipping container, the underwater facility housed 864 servers and operated for more than two years. The results were intriguing. According to Microsoft Research , servers in the underwater installation experienced a failure rate one-eighth that of a comparable land-based control group. The company suggested that a controlled environment, filled with dry nitrogen rather than ordinary air, could help explain the difference. The project demonstrated that underwater data centers were technically feasible. It did not, however, establish that they were commercially practical at scale. The problem with fixing a server at the bottom of the sea Imagine a hard drive fails in a conventional data center. A technician can walk over, replace it, and get the equipment running again. Now imagine that same failure several dozen meters underwater. The entire sealed module may need to be recovered, transported to the surface, opened, repaired, and redeployed. That is a rather expensive way to replace a component. Subsea facilities also need reliable power and high-capacity connections to land-based networks. Laying and maintaining undersea cables adds cost and complexity, while saltwater, pressure, corrosion, and marine conditions create additional engineering challenges. Microsoft’s experiment was successful in important technical respects, but the company eventually moved on. In June 2024, Data Center Dynamics reported that Microsoft had confirmed it was no longer pursuing subsea data centers. The company said it would apply lessons from the project to other areas of its operations. Cooling isn’t the whole business Another consideration is where the data center’s customers are. Cloud services, online gaming, financial transactions, and many AI applications depend on fast communication between users and servers. Placing a facility far from population centers and network hubs can increase latency, the time it takes for data to travel between devices and servers. That may not matter much for some large-scale computing tasks, but it can be important for applications that need near-instant responses. Then there is the economics. Data center operators must weigh land, construction, electricity, cooling, networking, staffing, maintenance, and regulatory costs over decades. A cheaper cooling system does not automatically make the entire facility cheaper to build and operate. The American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE) identifies power availability, grid capacity, cooling requirements, and permitting as important factors in data center site selection. The Arctic and the ocean will likely remain interesting options for specialized facilities, particularly where renewable energy, suitable network connections, and local infrastructure are available. But for now, the best place for a data center isn’t necessarily the coldest place on Earth. It is the place where the electricity, connectivity, cooling, maintenance, and economics all work together. Unfortunately for anyone hoping to put the cloud in an actual cloud of ice, geography is a little more complicated.

title: Kongsberg lands contract boost to expand underwater drone capabilities
content: Kongsberg Gruppen ASA will supply autonomous underwater vehicles and associated components under a $54 million contract modification from the Department of War Innovation Unit (DIU), extending its collaboration with the agency and the US Navy. The contract modifies an existing Prototype Other Transaction Agreement, with deliveries of a broad range of autonomous underwater vehicles accounting for most of its value. The company did not identify the vehicle models, quantities, delivery schedule or specific missions covered by the modification. The agreement adds to a year in which Kongsberg has signed AUV contracts worth NOK 1.7 billion ($184.6 million USD) across defense and commercial markets. The company said the latest contract supports its ambition to expand in undersea warfare. Expanded underwater deliveries The modification covers both autonomous vehicles and associated underwater capability components. Kongsberg did not provide a breakdown of the contract’s value between those categories or detail how the components would support the vehicles. The announcement identifies the delivery of underwater capabilities as the main driver of the modification. Its reference to a broad range of AUVs leaves the precise mix of platforms undisclosed. “This contract continues our collaboration with DIU and the US Navy and reflects confidence in KONGSBERG’s autonomous underwater technology. We remain focused on delivering reliable systems for demanding operational environments,” said CEO Eirik Lie. “It also demonstrates the value of our dual-use portfolio in delivering defense capabilities and further strengthens our position as a technology and defense company,” he added. Lie’s comments place the contract within the company’s existing relationship with its defense customers. He also highlighted the role of a portfolio serving both military and commercial requirements in supporting defense capability deliveries. Defense and commercial demand Kongsberg has more than 30 years of experience in autonomous underwater vehicles . It develops and delivers large AUV systems for defense and commercial customers worldwide, alongside its work on systems adapted for defense missions. Camilla Kiss, executive vice president of Kongsberg and president of its Discovery division, said the latest contract reflected continuing demand across both markets. “Autonomous underwater systems are a core part of KONGSBERG’s technology portfolio. So far in 2026, we have signed AUV contracts worth a total of NOK 1.7 billion across all markets. This progress supports our strategic ambition to grow in undersea warfare and strengthens the foundation for continued development,” she said . The NOK 1.7 billion figure covers contracts across all markets. It represents the broader AUV business described by Kiss, rather than the value of the DIU modification alone. AI and onboard processing Kiss also pointed to artificial intelligence, edge processing and autonomy as technologies changing what underwater platforms can undertake. Her comments described the direction of development across the company’s underwater portfolio; the announcement did not specify which technologies or configurations would be included in the latest deliveries. “Advances in artificial intelligence, edge processing and autonomy are enabling platforms to undertake increasingly complex missions with greater persistence and operational effectiveness. We are at the forefront of this development,” Kiss said. Kongsberg linked these advances to its continued development of autonomous underwater capabilities for defense and commercial customers.

title: Fish switch leaders 2.8 times a second to stay in sync, reveals a virtual reality study
content: Schooling fish switched the neighbor guiding their movements about 2.8 times a second in a virtual reality experiment, offering new insight into how they stay in sync. To investigate coordinated movements in fish, researchers chose the rummy-nose tetras ( Hemigrammus rhodostomus ) for the study, a species known for its schooling behavior. Using a closed-loop virtual reality system, real tetras interacted with digital fish that the researchers could control. The projector cast these images of virtual fish on the walls of a 52.2-centimeter bowl containing 15 liters of water. A depth camera tracked the real fish’s movement in three dimensions. “Collective motion in animal groups emerges from local interactions, yet how individuals select and integrate social information remains poorly understood,” the researchers said. Investigating schooling behavior Researchers programmed virtual fish to respond to their one, two, or four most influential neighbors. They conducted eight one-hour experiments for each setup. The team compared swimming speeds , distances between individuals, alignment, spatial organization, and turning behavior. They found that coordination increased when the virtual fish responded to more neighbors, the researchers stated in the study. “Groups became more cohesive, fish trajectories became smoother, and departures of the real fish from the virtual subgroup became less frequent.” Although the virtual schools became more cohesive when the programmed fish responded to more neighbors, however analyses showed the real fish behaved as if it primarily tracked a single influential neighbor. “The turning statistics provide a clear behavioral indicator that the dynamics of the real fish are best explained when it responds to a single most influential neighbor.” And this neighbor wasn’t always the closest fish either. Influential neighbors switch as they swim The most influential neighbor changed as the fish moved in sync. Researchers recorded an average switching frequency of about 2.8 times per second. Roughly 40 changes occurred between two consecutive spontaneous U-turns. “…Influential-neighbor switching reflects the continuous spatial reorganization of the group rather than periods of sustained leadership by particular individuals.” Fish coordinate their movements through changing interactions rather than relying on one leader. “Social influence is continuously redistributed as individuals move relative to one another, generating a rapidly evolving interaction network that nevertheless supports robust collective coordination,” the researchers said . Unlike the previous perspective, coordination doesn’t necessarily require integrating information from many neighbors simultaneously. Limitations of virtual reality The researchers acknowledged limitations in their experimental approach. Although the virtual fish responded visually to the movements of the real fish, they did not generate water movements or pressure disturbances. Researchers explained that fish are known to rely on multiple sensory pathways, such as vision, hydrodynamic cues, and pressure sensing through the lateral line system when coordinating their movements within schools. However, in the virtual-reality set up, the digital fish could only be perceived visually because they don’t generate water movements and pressure disturbances, which would need to be addressed in later experiments. In the future, the team would like to conduct their experiment on larger groups with the missing conditions built into the model. The results suggest the fish coordinated through continuously changing interactions rather than following a fixed leader. The research findings were published in PRX Life .

title: China's Humvee-like launcher could pack 12 ready-to-fire missiles
content: China’s short-range air defense system could be getting a significant upgrade, with reports suggesting its 4×4 launcher vehicle may soon carry three times as many ready-to-fire missiles.The speculation follows a social media post featuring images and video of what appears to be an updated version of China’s Yitian-L short-range air defense system on the move.Missile launch capacity tripledThe redesigned launcher was seen carrying two six-round missile packs instead of the four individual missile canisters used on earlier versions. As before, the launcher is mounted on the Dongfeng Mengshi 4×4, China’s equivalent of the Humvee, but now features two six-tube launch packs on the vehicle’s roof.The vehicle was photographed while being transported, although it remains unclear where and when the images were taken.It is also unknown whether the vehicle belongs to the Chinese military or represents an export variant. NORINCO, the state-owned defense manufacturer that builds the Yitian family of air defense systems, has not commented on the reported upgrade.“China knows its priority is building the Yitian-L air defense system for its people, not war,” the social media user wrote alongside the video of the Chinese Humvee.The Yitian system is designed to protect troops and fixed sites against low-flying helicopters, drones, and cruise missiles. In its current configuration, the lightweight Yitian-L carries four TY-90 infrared-guided missiles and a foldable 3D X-band radar mounted on the roof. NORINCO claims the radar can detect targets up to 11 miles (18 km) away. The TY-90 missiles have an engagement range of 500 m to 3.7 miles (6 km) and can intercept targets at altitudes of up to 2.48 miles (4 km). The system is operated by a two-person crew using a joystick-controlled digital console from inside the vehicle.Could tackle drone swarmsIt is also unclear whether the additional missiles are standard TY-90s or a smaller derivative. The TY-90 was originally developed as a short-range air-to-air missile for Chinese helicopters before being adapted for ground launch with a passive infrared guidance system that tracks targets using their heat signatures. Because the missiles are fire-and-forget weapons, the launcher does not need to continuously illuminate the target, helping reduce the chances of revealing the vehicle’s position during combat. The available images also do not show whether the upgraded Yitian-L retains the same radar and fire-control system or whether the increased missile load affects its range or performance.A launcher carrying 12 missiles could help address a challenge highlighted in recent conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, where swarms of small drones can rapidly exhaust four-missile launchers. The original Yitian and the newer Yitian II, both mounted on armored personnel carriers, carry eight TY-90 missiles each. If confirmed, a 12-round Yitian-L would exceed the missile capacity of either heavier variant.So far, the Yitian-L has primarily been marketed as an export product.

title: US ally gets new warship with 21-cell missile defense system
content: Greece has received HS Nearchos, its second Defense and Intervention Frigate, adding a warship with expanded air defenses to the Hellenic Navy’s fleet. Naval Group handed over the vessel on October 30 at its Lorient shipyard in France.The delivery took place in the presence of Greek Defense Minister Nikos Dendias and French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin. Nearchos follows HS Kimon, delivered in December 2025, as Greece advances its FDI frigate program. The new ship arrives with additional weapons under the Standard 2 configuration, strengthening its ability to defend against aerial threats. Additional weapons strengthen air defensesNearchos differs from the lead ship in the combat capabilities included in its delivery configuration.Its Standard 2 equipment includes two additional A50 SYLVER vertical launch system modules, four SYLENA Mk1 decoy launchers, and a 21-cell Rolling Airframe Missile system for close-in defense.These additions form the main weapons upgrade over the initial Standard 1 configuration. The distinction also concerns how the equipment is integrated with the ship’s combat management system.Kimon has been fitted with additional weapons, but Naval News reports that full installation and integration with its SETIS combat management system, bringing it to Standard 2, will be completed by October 2027.The frigates also feature the SEAFIRE multifunction radar, SENTINEL electronic support system, and PASEO XLR electro-optical fire-control equipment.Further upgrades planned for the fleetThe delivery configuration is one stage in a broader development plan for the Kimon-class frigates. Naval News reports that Nearchos is scheduled to reach Standard 2++ in April 2029.Subsequent upgrades include changes to the SETIS combat management system, sensors, electronic equipment, and asymmetric warfare center. Plans also cover full integration of the S-100 CAMCOPTER unmanned aircraft and enhanced weapons capabilities.A potential later configuration could replace one forward A50 launcher module with an A70 module capable of accommodating naval cruise missiles. That remains a possible future development rather than equipment included in the current delivery. Industrial partnership supports long-term operationsBeyond the handover, Naval Group’s announcement outlines the industrial arrangements supporting Greece’s frigate program, which began in 2022.More than 75 Greek companies participate across the company’s FDI frigate and submarine programs. Their work includes electronic maps, pre-armed ship blocks, and complex mechanical and electronic systems. That figure covers both programs, rather than the frigates alone.The Hellenic Navy has also awarded Naval Group the initial in-service support contract for its FDI vessels. Maintenance and upgrades will involve the company, its Greek subsidiary Naval Group Hellas, and local industrial partners.“Only ten months after the delivery of HS Kimon, it is an honor to deliver the second FDI frigate,” Naval Group Chairman and CEO Pierre Éric Pommellet said.Naval Group said the third frigate, HS Formion, is planned for delivery by the end of 2026. Under that schedule, Greece would receive three FDI frigates within roughly a year of Kimon’s handover. The support partnership provides the arrangements for maintaining and upgrading the ships throughout their service.

title: 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles approved as US boosts Ukraine defense
content: Lockheed Martin, a major defense supplier, is likely to supply Ukraine with 500 Patriot air defense interceptor missiles after the US State Department approved the potential sale Friday, October 30.​According to the press statement, the approval came following a request from the government of Ukraine to purchase Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) missiles to improve its integrated air and missile defense capabilities.​Patriot’s PAC-3 MSE variant, manufactured by Lockheed Martin, is one of the most advanced, high-velocity surface-to-air missile interceptors capable of shooting down incoming ballistic missiles. Ukraine, allies backs purchase​The estimated cost of purchase for these 500 missiles is estimated at $2.1 billion. Ukrainian national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan and donations from allies including Canada, Germany and Norway through the US JUMPSTART program will be used to make the purchase, the State Department said. No U.S. funds will be used to make the purchase, the statement added.​Under the agreement, the company will supply PAC-3 MSE classified and unclassified spare parts and other related logistics and program support elements.​ However, the U.S. government did not comment on when the Ukrainian military will receive these crucial defensive weapons.​Lockheed Martin, the principal contractor for the newly approved missile sale, is already in talks with allied nations to establish PAC-3 production outside the US, as the demand for the interceptor surges globally.​By 2030, the company plans to expand its annual production capacity, up from 600 missiles to 2000, while investing in 20 facilities on the American soil.​PAC3 Edge to combat hypersonic weaponsIn addition to greenlighting the sale of 500 Patriot air missiles to Ukraine, the U.S. Army also awarded a nearly $1.1 billion contract to Lockheed Martin to develop PAC-3 Edge, an advanced interceptor technology. The new combat technology is expected to expand air- and missile-defense coverage against advanced threats, including hypersonic weapons. These missiles, with greater engagement range and altitude, are designed to replace PAC-3 MSE and THAAD.​Built on combat-proven PAC-3 MSE, PAC-3 Edge will have a new seeker, improved propulsion, and upgraded controls. These engineering changes are intended to improve precision, maneuverability, and performance at greater ranges and altitudes, a company official said.​The seeker of the advanced missile system is tasked with tracking targets during the engagement, while the propulsion determines the energy available along the flight path, and control systems enable the missile to adjust its trajectory. The combined effectiveness of these systems will determine if PAC-3 Edge can meet its proposed engagement envelope against maneuvering targets, noted the company officials.​However, no official announcements provided a number for PAC-3 Edge’s interception ranges, altitude limits, seeker operating characteristics, or demonstrated performance against representative hypersonic targets.​The latest development award marks progress toward expanding the defensive capability. However, whether PAC-3 Edge delivers the proposed improvement against advanced missile and hypersonic threats will depend on the results of its development, testing, and integration program.​

title: Chery Tiggo 2 gets 0 Stars in Latin NCAP Crash Test
content: Chinese automaker Chery is facing renewed questions about vehicle safety after its Tiggo 2 compact SUV received a zero-star rating in the latest Latin NCAP crash tests. The assessment found an unstable body structure and footwell during frontal impact, poor protection for the driver’s chest and a fire risk that contributed to the vehicle scoring zero for adult occupant protection.The results also gave the Tiggo 2 zero points for child occupant protection. The SUV, sold in different markets as the Tiggo 2 Pro, Tiggo 2 Pro Max and Chirey Tiggo 2, comes with four airbags and electronic stability control as standard. It nevertheless achieved just 48.89 percent for pedestrian protection and 45.45 percent for safety assistance systems. The result adds to scrutiny of Chery’s quality controls as the company expands its presence in overseas markets, including Latin America and Southeast Asia.Unstable structure, fire risk Latin NCAP evaluated the Tiggo 2 through frontal and side-impact tests, whiplash assessments, pedestrian protection tests and evaluations of its electronic stability control and emergency maneuvering performance.During the frontal impact, the vehicle’s body structure and footwell area were both rated as unstable. The driver’s chest showed poor protection, with high compression recorded during the collision. Latin NCAP also identified a fire risk during the test, which contributed to the zero-point result for adult occupant protection.The absence of standard side head-protection airbags meant the vehicle was not subjected to the side pole impact test, resulting in an additional penalty. The assessment also found that the rear seats lacked seatbelt pretensioners and load limiters, while the vehicle could not demonstrate adequate protection for a smaller adult passenger in the second row.Child occupant protection was equally concerning, with Latin NCAP awarding the Tiggo 2 zero points after identifying problems in both dynamic crash testing and child restraint system installation. The assessment recorded high forces on the head and neck of the 10-year-old test dummy during frontal and side impacts, while the 3-year-old dummy faced head exposure and a risk of ejection in the side-impact test.Previous quality lapsesAccording to Alejandro Furas, Latin NCAP’s secretary general, the result puts Chery in the spotlight for offering low safety performance in a popular vehicle segment. The organization also argued that mandatory safety labelling based on independent crash-test results could help consumers make better-informed purchasing decisions.The crash-test result comes weeks after Chery encountered another quality issue in Malaysia, where an Omoda 5 experienced a rear axle assembly separation earlier in October. The incident prompted Malaysia’s Road Transport Department to temporarily suspend the model’s Vehicle Type Approval, halting new registrations while the issue was addressed.Chery subsequently initiated a recall covering 8,878 Omoda 5 C and H variants. Chairman and president Yin Tongyue also apologized for the quality concerns during the World Intelligent Connected Vehicles Conference on October 21, saying the company needed to establish itself in overseas markets rather than pursue short-term gains.The incidents involve different vehicle models and separate technical problems, but they come at a time when Chinese automakers are expanding rapidly beyond their domestic market. Chery has exported vehicles to more than 80 countries and regions, and the Tiggo 2 is among its entry-level models aimed at markets across Southeast Asia, Latin America and the Middle East.

title: UK plans 3 advanced undersea sensor systems for AUKUS submarine fleets
content: The UK will lead the development of three advanced undersea payloads for uncrewed underwater vehicles (UUVs) operated by Australia, the UK, and the US under the AUKUS security partnership. The technologies are designed to help autonomous underwater systems map the ocean floor, detect potential threats, and deploy underwater effects. Availability across the three nations’ fleets is expected from 2027.The announcement follows a week of demonstrations at the Maritime Big Play-Pacific exercise in San Diego, where allied forces tested how crewed and uncrewed maritime systems could operate together. The work forms part of the first signature project under AUKUS Pillar II, which focuses on developing advanced capabilities through cooperation between the three countries.The UK will lead the development and delivery of three payloads: a Synthetic Aperture Sonar (SAS), a Deployable Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) Sensor, and a Deployable Non-Kinetic Effector.Three payloads for underwater surveillanceThe three systems are intended to give uncrewed underwater vehicles a broader range of sensing and operational capabilities. Synthetic Aperture Sonar uses acoustic signals to produce detailed images of the seabed and underwater objects. By combining measurements collected as a vehicle moves, the technology can create higher-resolution images than conventional sonar systems, helping operators examine large underwater areas and identify objects of interest.The Deployable Anti-Submarine Warfare Sensor takes a different approach. Rather than relying only on sensors carried by a vehicle, it is designed to deploy sensing equipment into the water to detect and classify underwater threats. Such distributed sensors could help expand surveillance coverage and improve the ability to monitor potential submarine activity.The third payload, a Deployable Non-Kinetic Effector, is intended to generate effects underwater without relying on conventional kinetic weapons. The UK Ministry of Defense has not disclosed its precise technical configuration or the specific effects it will produce.Together, the payloads are intended to help UUVs conduct wider-area surveillance and contribute to the protection of critical underwater infrastructure, including subsea cables and other strategically important assets.AUKUS tests autonomous systems in San DiegoThe development announcement followed Maritime Big Play-Pacific, an exercise designed to test how autonomous maritime technologies can be integrated into allied operations before wider deployment.The exercise covered four areas: anti-submarine warfare, lethality, contested resupply, and subsea and seabed warfare. The UK led the anti-submarine warfare strand, contributing 13 uncrewed surface vehicles, two ASW targets, and four underwater gliders supplied by six industry partners.The demonstrations also focused on the control systems needed to coordinate different autonomous platforms. Getting underwater vehicles, surface drones, and crewed naval vessels to exchange information and operate together is essential if uncrewed systems are to become a meaningful part of future naval operations.The UK Ministry of Defense described the effort as part of its planned transition toward a Hybrid Navy, combining crewed warships and submarines with autonomous and uncrewed platforms.The project also involves a wider industrial network. UK companies SEA Ltd, Decision Analysis Services Ltd, and A2i, alongside US-based MSI Transducers, were selected through the AUKUS Maritime Innovation Challenge. The four suppliers share £3 million (approximately $4 million) in funding to develop technologies for the command, control, and cooperation of undersea systems.Expanding underwater capabilitiesThe new payloads build on other recent AUKUS milestones in autonomous underwater warfare. Earlier in October, a US-Australian heavyweight torpedo was successfully test-fired from the UK’s extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicle, XV Excalibur. The demonstration marked the first such firing from an uncrewed submarine.The developments reflect growing interest in using autonomous platforms to extend naval surveillance and operations across large maritime areas. Uncrewed systems can potentially remain deployed for extended periods, cover areas that would be difficult to monitor continuously with crewed vessels, and reduce the need to expose personnel to dangerous missions.With the three new sensor payloads expected to become available across AUKUS fleets from 2027, the partnership is moving toward a more integrated network of autonomous maritime capabilities. The challenge will be turning individual demonstrations and technologies into systems that can reliably operate together in real-world conditions.

title: US Navy pushes next-generation warships plan to strengthen superiority
content: The US Navy is pursuing an ambitious shipbuilding expansion, from new nuclear-powered aircraft carriers and submarines to redesigned surface combatants and a proposed class of battleships. But as the service expands its fleet, construction delays, maintenance backlogs, and limited shipyard capacity continue to complicate its plans.One of the clearest signs of progress came on September 29, when the Navy took preliminary acceptance of the future USS John F. Kennedy (CVN 79), its second Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier. The milestone allows the ship and its crew to conduct further at-sea testing while its builder, Newport News Shipbuilding, completes remaining work. The Navy said the carrier was approximately 99% complete, with formal delivery expected in spring 2027.According to the US Navy’s announcement, testing of four remaining advanced weapons elevators was among the work still to be completed. Preliminary acceptance marks progress toward delivery, but does not mean the carrier is fully operational.Carriers, submarines and destroyers anchor fleet renewalThe Ford-class program represents the Navy’s effort to modernize its carrier fleet, while the Virginia-class and Columbia-class submarine programs address different undersea requirements. Virginia-class boats conduct attack-submarine missions, including intelligence gathering and strikes against enemy targets. The Columbia class is being developed to replace the Navy’s aging Ohio-class ballistic missile submarines, which form a central part of the US nuclear deterrent.The Navy is also continuing to build Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyers. The latest Flight III configuration features the AN/SPY-6(V)1 radar, designed to improve air and missile defense capabilities. Together, these programs underpin the fleet’s ability to project power, protect carrier groups, and conduct operations across multiple maritime theaters.However, building new vessels is only part of the challenge. A Government Accountability Office report published in August 2026 found that maintenance delays and idle time for attack submarines cost the Navy more than 15,000 operational days over the previous decade, with an estimated $3.4 billion spent sustaining submarines and crews that provided no operational capability.The findings emphasize a bigger problem. Adding ships to the construction pipeline does not automatically translate into more vessels available for deployment.Frigates and battleships signal a changing approachThe Navy is also reconsidering how it builds smaller surface combatants. In November 2025, it announced a major restructuring of the Constellation-class frigate program. Under the revised approach, construction of the first two ships would continue, while the Navy canceled four additional ships in the existing program. The Navy has instead pursued a new FF(X) frigate initiative based on the Coast Guard’s National Security Cutter design.The shift reflects concerns about the original program’s schedule, design complexity, and cost. The Navy’s Constellation-class fact file outlines the revised program status. At the other end of the surface fleet, the administration is proposing a new class of nuclear-powered guided-missile battleships, designated BBGN. The scale of the plan illustrates the competing demands facing the shipbuilding industry.In its assessment of the Navy’s new battleship program, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that building 15 ships between 2028 and 2056 could cost approximately $275 billion in 2026 dollars. The first vessel alone could cost about $23 billion. These are independent estimates of a proposed procurement program, not money already spent or a finalized construction bill.The CBO also warned that the Navy’s plans would substantially increase the tonnage of large surface combatants shipyards must produce, potentially creating a significant industrial challenge.Shipyard capacity could determine the outcomeThe Navy’s fiscal year 2027 shipbuilding plan requests a major investment in fleet expansion and the maritime industrial base. Released in May, the plan calls for $65.8 billion in shipbuilding investment and emphasizes workforce development, shipyard capacity, and improved delivery performance. The Navy’s announcement describes the administration’s long-term fleet ambitions, but proposed spending and future procurement should not be confused with completed construction.The infrastructure challenge extends beyond shipbuilding yards to facilities responsible for maintaining the existing fleet. A September 2026 GAO report estimated that the Navy’s Shipyard Infrastructure Optimization Program could exceed $200 billion and take more than 50 additional years to complete under current plans.The scale of these requirements explains why expanding the fleet will require more than larger budgets. The Navy must also improve production schedules, modernize shipyards, train workers, and keep existing vessels available for service.The coming years will test whether the United States can turn its shipbuilding ambitions into a larger, more capable fleet. New carriers, submarines, and surface combatants remain central to that effort, but their strategic value will ultimately depend on whether the industrial base can deliver them on time and keep them ready for operations.
