title: Keeping homes powered in a blackout: 2 battery options compared
content: A blackout forces households to decide what needs electricity first: the refrigerator, a few lights, or the heating system. A home battery and a portable power station can both supply stored energy, but they differ in how they deliver it and how much installation they require.For households choosing backup power, the decision comes down to which appliances must run, how long outages typically last, and whether the system needs to work automatically. A portable station can suit selected devices, while an installed home battery can support circuits throughout the house, depending on its configuration.How the two systems deliver backup powerA home battery connects to the household electrical system through an inverter and associated control equipment. In a backup-capable installation, that equipment disconnects the home from the grid during an outage and supplies designated circuits from the battery. Depending on system design, coverage can include selected essential loads or the entire home. A portable power station packages battery storage, an inverter, and outlets into a unit that supplies appliances plugged directly into it. This makes it useful for powering individual devices without installing a permanent battery system.The distinction is becoming less rigid, however. Some larger portable stations support expansion batteries and can connect to household circuits through compatible transfer equipment. Buyers therefore need to compare the actual configuration. A portable unit connected to a home panel involves different equipment and installation requirements from one used simply to charge phones.Capacity determines runtime, while output limits appliancesTwo specifications matter: energy capacity and power output. Capacity, measured in watt-hours or kilowatt-hours, indicates how much energy the battery can store. Output, measured in watts or kilowatts, determines how much load equipment can operate simultaneously.California’s Air Resources Board emphasizes that backup batteries must be sized for both demand and runtime.Consider a simplified example: a battery delivering 1 kilowatt-hour (1,000 watt-hours) to appliances could support a constant 100-watt load for 10 hours. Actual runtime depends on conversion losses, the available charge, and how appliances cycle.Starting demand also matters. A refrigerator or pump may briefly require more power when their motor starts. Check the backup system’s continuous and surge ratings against the appliances it must operate.A larger battery does not automatically mean every appliance can run together. Tesla advises Powerwall owners to manage high-consumption equipment during outages because combined demand can exceed the system’s power rating. Reducing those loads also extends runtime.Which option makes more sense?For a renter or a household covering occasional short outages, a portable station is a practical starting point when the priority is a few essential plug-in appliances. Compare its purchase price, usable capacity, output, weight, and charging options.An installed home battery deserves closer consideration when automatic backup and hardwired appliances are priorities. Compare complete installed quotes, including electrical work and backup controls, rather than battery prices alone.For extended blackouts, recharging becomes decisive. Both options eventually exhaust their stored energy unless another source replenishes it. Compatible solar panels can help, but production depends on sunlight and system capabilities.Existing rooftop solar does not automatically provide power during blackouts. The US Department of Energy explains that conventional grid-connected solar generally shuts down during outages; continued operation requires an appropriately configured inverter and storage system.Start with an appliance list and a realistic outage duration. If a few outlets cover those needs, portability may be sufficient. If the requirement extends to automatic circuit-level backup, an installed system may justify the additional work.

title: Northrop Grumman secures $56 million for Triton drone upgrade
content: Northrop Grumman will upgrade a single U.S. Navy MQ-4C Triton maritime surveillance drone under a nearly $56 million contract modification awarded on October 28. The work covers installation of a B7 retrofit material kit and is scheduled for completion in May 2030.Naval Air Systems Command awarded the firm-fixed-price modification without competition, committing the full $55,986,538 from fiscal 2027 aircraft procurement funds. The announcement does not identify the aircraft receiving the kit or explain what equipment, software, or capabilities the installation will change.Upgrade details remain undisclosedNorthrop Grumman will perform 64 percent of the work in Palmdale, California, where Triton aircraft are built. Another 34 percent will take place in San Diego, with the remaining 2 percent distributed across other U.S. locations.The B7 designation follows the numbering used for individual Triton airframes in earlier contracts. However, the Navy has not confirmed whether this installation will bring the aircraft to the Integrated Functional Capability 4 standard, commonly called IFC-4.Previous contracts explicitly identified that configuration. A 2023 award worth $83.1 million covered upgrades to air vehicles B9 and B10, along with a main operating base, to the multi-intelligence standard.The latest contract also resembles earlier work on air vehicle B5. In late 2025, the Navy exercised a $45.75 million option covering engineering, tooling, and labor to complete IFC-4 changes on that aircraft. That work had the same geographic split and a June 2029 completion target.Sensors expand Triton’s intelligence roleIFC-4 introduced signals intelligence capabilities to Triton through additional sensors for electronic intelligence and communications intelligence, according to Northrop Grumman.The sensors brought stricter requirements for protecting collected data, prompting hardware and software changes across the aircraft and its ground systems. The Navy first flew a Triton in the IFC-4 configuration on July 29, 2021.Other surveillance equipment includes the AN/ZPY-3 Multi-Function Active Sensor, an X-band electronically scanned radar mounted beneath the fuselage, and the Raytheon AN/DAS-3 electro-optical and infrared turret.Triton’s structure also differs substantially from the RQ-4 Global Hawk on which it is based. Northrop strengthened the airframe and wings and added de-icing equipment and lightning protection.Those changes allow the unarmed aircraft to descend from approximately 50,000 feet to around 10,000 feet to identify ships before returning to its higher patrol altitude.Further fleet changes take shapeThe latest contract follows another October order worth $66 million to install 17 U.S. Navy and 16 Australian engineering changes on operational Tritons.Separately, Naval Air Systems Command posted an October 22 notice outlining plans for a sole-source contract with Northrop Grumman covering engineering, software and cyber sustainment, logistics, and engineering change proposals.That proposed agreement would support both the U.S. Navy and Royal Australian Air Force, with an award expected in the third quarter of fiscal 2027.Australia acquires Tritons through a cooperative program covering development, production, and sustainment. Meanwhile, the B7 installation remains narrowly defined in the public announcement: a funded upgrade to one aircraft, with its precise technical scope and resulting configuration still undisclosed by the Navy.

title: NASA’s Swift telescope to fall back to Earth after 21 years in orbit
content: After more than 21 years watching some of the universe’s most violent events, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has reached the end of its mission. The spacecraft is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere in the coming weeks, but its scientific legacy is far from over. Researchers will continue mining its enormous archive of observations for years, potentially uncovering discoveries long after the telescope itself is gone.NASA announced on October 23 that Swift had ended science operations after its orbit dropped too low for the spacecraft to reliably point its telescopes at astronomical targets. Its final observation took place on October 20, when it was orbiting approximately 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth.The observatory was originally designed for a two-year mission. Instead, it operated for more than a decade beyond that planned lifetime, observing everything from distant stellar explosions to black holes and objects in our own solar system.A telescope built to chase cosmic explosionsLaunched on November 20, 2004, Swift was designed primarily to detect gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), brief but extraordinarily energetic flashes associated with some of the most powerful events in the universe.These bursts can last from fractions of a second to several minutes. Their fleeting nature makes them hard to study. Astronomers must locate them quickly and turn other telescopes toward the source before the light fades.Swift was built to do exactly that. Its Burst Alert Telescope detects gamma-ray bursts and determines their positions, allowing the spacecraft to rapidly turn its X-ray and ultraviolet/optical telescopes toward the event. NASA says the observatory could typically redirect its instruments within about a minute.That rapid-response capability helped transform the study of gamma-ray bursts and made Swift a valuable tool for time-domain astronomy, which examines how astronomical objects change over time.Over its lifetime, the spacecraft observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and studied over 1,400 supernova explosions. It also monitored active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes, observed stars being torn apart by black holes, and studied comets and asteroids.One notable observation came in 2022, when Swift helped investigate GRB 221009A, nicknamed the BOAT (Brightest Of All Time). The extraordinary burst of radiation became one of the brightest gamma-ray events ever detected.An attempted rescue couldn’t save the observatorySwift’s descent accelerated due to increased solar activity. When the Sun becomes more active, it heats Earth’s upper atmosphere, causing it to expand. That increases atmospheric drag on satellites in low Earth orbit, gradually slowing them down and reducing their altitude.NASA attempted to extend Swift’s life through an unusual servicing mission. The agency contracted Arizona-based Katalyst Space Technologies to develop a robotic spacecraft called LINK, designed to rendezvous with Swift, capture it, and raise its orbit.LINK launched on July 3, 2026, aboard Northrop Grumman’s Pegasus XL rocket. However, an attitude-control problem prevented the spacecraft from capturing or boosting Swift. NASA announced in August that the orbit-raising attempt would not proceed, although LINK would continue demonstrating rendezvous and proximity-operation capabilities.With Swift continuing to lose altitude, its science operations eventually became unsustainable. NASA ended the mission after the spacecraft entered safe mode on October 20.A 12-terabyte scientific legacyAlthough Swift is about to disappear from orbit, its observations will remain accessible to researchers. NASA says the mission has produced approximately 12 terabytes of data, including nearly 22 years of brightness measurements, multiwavelength spectra, and more than 1.5 million images from its Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope.The archive has already contributed to approximately 7,000 scientific papers. Its value could continue growing as astronomers revisit older observations, combine them with newer measurements, and apply improved analytical techniques.NASA’s Swift archive makes the mission’s observations publicly accessible, allowing researchers around the world to explore its data.Swift’s departure will nevertheless leave a gap. NASA is exploring ways to maintain rapid-response observations of cosmic events using existing space telescopes and potentially new commercial capabilities.For a spacecraft that spent more than two decades chasing some of the universe’s briefest and most energetic flashes, its final chapter is fittingly unusual. Swift may soon burn up in Earth’s atmosphere, but the cosmic events it captured will remain available for astronomers to study long after its last signal is gone.

title: Robotic moth grows its own sensors with UV light and artificial blood
content: Imagine sending a robot into an unfamiliar environment without knowing what it might encounter. If it comes across something its existing sensors cannot detect, it would normally need to return to a workshop for new equipment. But what if it could instead grow a new sensor right where it needs one?A team of researchers has demonstrated a step toward this possibility with a moth-shaped robot that uses an artificial circulatory system to transport chemical ingredients through its body and grow a functioning light sensor wherever ultraviolet (UV) light strikes. “I’m working on giving robots a circulatory system, so they can transport molecular building blocks across the whole body and create the hardware they need, on site, where and when it’s needed,” Kadri-Ann Pankratov, lead researcher and a PhD student at the University of Tartu in Estonia, said.The experiment suggests that robots could eventually adapt not just by changing how they use existing hardware, but by chemically creating entirely new capabilities within their bodies.Taking a cue from how insects circulate materialsMost robots leave the factory with their hardware already decided. Engineers must anticipate which sensors they will need and where to install them. Although adaptive software can help robots respond to unexpected situations, it cannot compensate for a missing physical sensor. Adding entirely new capabilities after deployment remains a significant engineering challenge.The researchers from the University of Tartu in Estonia and the Italian Institute of Technology explored whether a robot could overcome this limitation by borrowing an idea from nature: circulation. In insects, an open circulatory system pumps hemolymph, a blood-like fluid, through the body, allowing it to reach different organs and tissues.The team took inspiration from moths, particularly the blue underwing (Catocala fraxini). Its relatively flat wings offered a convenient model because their circulation happens largely in a single plane, simplifying the robot’s internal plumbing.The researchers 3D-printed a transparent plastic body using polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG). Each of its two wings covered 86 square centimeters and contained millimeter-wide channels resembling veins. Smaller gaps between the printed plastic lines formed a network of microchannels, allowing liquids to penetrate about 10 micrometers into the material. A single pump circulated around 3 milliliters (ml) of liquid throughout the robot, distributing chemical ingredients across its body.UV light turns part of robot into a sensorTo create a light receptor, the researchers circulated an artificial hemolymph containing pyrrole, a light-activated chemical initiator, and a cellulose-based additive called cellulose acetate propionate (CAP). The mixture entered the plastic’s internal microchannels and infused the surrounding material.When UV light struck a particular area for approximately one minute, it triggered a chemical reaction that converted pyrrole into polypyrrole, an electrically conductive polymer. The previously transparent plastic gradually turned black wherever the reaction occurred, providing visible evidence of the newly formed material.Using a stencil, the researchers could control the sensor’s shape and position with a precision of 0.3 millimeters.The resulting material responded to UV exposure by temporarily changing its electrical properties. When UV light hit it, its electrical impedance dropped, allowing an onboard microcontroller to detect the signal. The robot could then respond by flapping its wings using a shape-memory wire or flashing an LED.In other words, the robot acquired a sensing ability it did not possess when it was manufactured.“You can, of course, use a ready-made photodiode, but you’d have to know quite precisely where to put it. That can be difficult to know beforehand as robots go into more dangerous and complicated environments. Growing the receptor on site means the environment itself can pattern the robot, based on what is actually happening at that time,” ,” Pankratov said.The researchers also noticed something unexpected: the sensor became increasingly sensitive with repeated UV exposure. Residual pyrrole continued polymerizing, creating additional polypyrrole structures and changing the sensor’s electrical properties. The team interprets this as a form of material memory, in which the sensor’s physical structure retains a record of its previous experiences. Remarkably, the sensors remained functional after more than four months of storage.Will robots grow their own hardware?The demonstration is still a proof of concept. It relies on a single predetermined chemical reaction, and sensor formation is irreversible. Researchers also controlled when the chemical mixture entered the robot and used a stencil to determine where the sensor developed. Plus, the robot cannot yet independently decide which new hardware it needs or invent a way to manufacture it.Nevertheless, the approach could eventually help robots operating in unfamiliar environments, from forests and collapsed buildings to underwater locations and other planets. The same circulatory network could transport different chemicals to produce materials for corrosion protection, electromagnetic shielding, or even interfaces with living tissue. Researchers also hope to explore chemical systems that could be reversible.The next challenge is making the process less dependent on predetermined instructions. “Right now, the robot’s central intelligence knew which component was coming. How do we make it so that it doesn’t have to be predetermined? We don’t yet have a good source of inspiration in biology for that,” Pankratov said.Pankratov hopes that artificial blood and circulatory systems could become an established option in robotics within the next decade, potentially allowing machines to develop capabilities in response to the environments they encounter.The study is published in the journal Advanced Science.

title: 10 massive Battery storage projects around the world
content: Storing electricity at the scale of several gigawatt-hours is becoming a reality for power grids around the world.From a solar-powered development in Abu Dhabi to battery installations across Saudi Arabia, these projects are designed to store electricity and supply it when it is needed.The following list includes individual facilities, multi-site programs, and phased developments, with capacities reflecting their published scope.Some are already operating, others remain under development, and Moss Landing illustrates why historical capacity must be distinguished from what a facility can deliver today.1. Masdar–EWEC round-the-clock project, UAE -19 GWhMasdarAbu Dhabi’s Masdar–EWEC development combines a 5.2-gigawatt solar plant with 19 gigawatt-hours of battery storage. The project is designed to deliver 1 gigawatt of renewable electricity around the clock, extending solar power delivery beyond daylight hours.Masdar laid the foundation for the project in October 2025, with operations targeted for 2027. Its design includes grid-forming technology, black-start capability, and forecasting and dispatch systems to coordinate electricity generation, storage, and delivery.2. SEC–BYD battery storage program, Saudi Arabia – 12.5 GWhBYD announced a 12.5-gigawatt-hour energy storage contract with Saudi Electricity Company in February 2025.The agreement covers multiple grid-scale projects and brings BYD’s combined Saudi cooperation with the utility to 15.1 gigawatt-hours, including an earlier 2.6-gigawatt-hour delivery.MEED identifies the program as five facilities with a combined power rating of 2.5 gigawatts, built with Alfanar as the engineering, procurement, and construction contractor.Equipment supplier NR Electric reported that SEC’s five-region, 2.5-gigawatt storage project completed its grid-connected charging and discharging tests on May 27, 2026, marking commissioning.3. Oasis de Atacama, Chile – 14.1 GWh (overall platform)Grenergy’s Oasis de Atacama is a phased solar and battery storage development in Chile. Although earlier plans set its storage capacity at about 11 gigawatt-hours, the company’s September 2026 announcement raised the overall platform a capacity to 14.1 gigawatt-hours.That figure reflects the wider development, with individual phases coming online separately.Grenergy confirmed in September 2026 that Gabriela, the fourth phase, was operational with 272 megawatts of solar generation and 1,100 megawatt-hours of battery storage.4. Najran, Khamis Mushait, and Madaya storage program, Saudi Arabia – 7.8 GWhSaudi Arabia’s 7.8-gigawatt-hour storage deployment spans three sites at Najran, Khamis Mushait, and Madaya. Sungrow supplied more than 1,500 PowerTitan 2.0 systems and announced grid connection completion in December 2025.The equipment integrates batteries, power conversion systems, medium-voltage transformers, and switching equipment into preassembled units. Sungrow says factory testing and preassembly reduced on-site installation work, while a local service team supported installation, commissioning, and grid connection.5. Envision Jingyi Chagan Hada, China – 4 GWhThe Envision Jingyi Chagan Hada Energy Storage Power Station in Inner Mongolia has a reported capacity of 4 gigawatt-hours. It connected to the grid in late December 2025, forming part of Envision’s wider 12.8-gigawatt-hour regional storage cluster.According to the Sustainable Markets Initiative’s project showcase, the station passed the grid’s three-charge, three-discharge verification in a single attempt.Its control system combines forecasting, dispatch, and electricity-market trading, coordinating how stored energy is managed and sold.6. Edwards & Sanborn, USA – 3.287 GWhCalifornia’s Edwards & Sanborn project combines solar generation with 3.287 gigawatt-hours of battery storage. Developer Terra-Gen and contractor Mortenson announced substantial completion of the Kern County development in January 2024.The installation spans more than 4,600 acres, with part of the project on Edwards Air Force Base.Mortenson identifies LG Chem, Samsung, and BYD as battery suppliers, while the project serves customers including California utilities, the city of San Jose, and Starbucks.7. Moss Landing, USA – 3 GWh (historical installed capacity)Wikimedia CommonsVistra’s Moss Landing Energy Storage Facility reached 750 megawatts and 3,000 megawatt-hours of installed capacity after its third expansion entered commercial operation in June 2023.That expansion added 350 megawatts and 1,400 megawatt-hours, establishing the California site as a major early example of multi-gigawatt-hour battery storage.Its historical capacity requires qualification following the January 2025 fire at the 300-megawatt facility.EPA confirms that the affected building has had no active battery storage operations since that incident, while Vistra subsequently decided not to return the separate 100-megawatt facility to service.8. Collie Battery, Australia – 2.24 GWhCollie BatteryNeoen’s Collie Battery in Western Australia has a combined capacity of 560 megawatts and 2,240 megawatt-hours. The development comprises a 219-megawatt first stage and a 341-megawatt second stage; the company’s October 2025 update said both are operational.The service addresses electricity reliability risks associated with coal-plant retirements, growing rooftop solar generation, and demand on Western Australia’s South-West Interconnected System.9. Bisha BESS, Saudi Arabia – 2 GWhThe Bisha battery storage facility in Saudi Arabia’s Aseer province is rated at 500 megawatts and 2,000 megawatt-hours.Contractor Alfanar describes the delivered installation as a four-hour system that stores electricity during low-demand periods for redistribution when demand rises.Bisha has also demonstrated a capability needed after a major grid outage: black start, or restoring power without relying on an already energized network.NR Electric reported a successful black-start test in February 2026 using its integrated power conversion, power management, and energy management systems.10. Huadian Xinjiang Kashgar, China – 2 GWh (first phase)The first phase of Huadian’s Kashgar energy storage project in Xinjiang has a capacity of 500 megawatts and 2,000 megawatt-hours.A Huadian Xinjiang account published by the China Energy Storage Alliance confirms that the first storage block entered grid-connected operation in July 2025.The installation uses 100 lithium iron phosphate storage units and combines grid-forming and conventional storage configurations, each accounting for half its capacity.State Grid Kashgar said the project supports renewable electricity use and grid stability in a region where photovoltaic generation represents a substantial share of installed power capacity.ConclusionThese projects show how battery storage is expanding from individual installations to multi-site programs measured in gigawatt-hours.Their engineering challenges extend beyond capacity to grid integration, reliable operation, and safety. As more facilities enter service, how consistently they store and deliver electricity will matter as much as their size.

title: US firm's next stealth drone could deliver 60-hour exceptional endurance
content: General Atomics (GA) has announced that it is in the process of designing a new flying-wing drone called NextGen. Intended for reconnaissance and strike missions, the new drone will also help inform the development of the company’s existing Gambit family of combat drones.What is of particular interest is the planned drone’s propulsion system. Rather than relying solely on a conventional jet engine or turboprop, General Atomics is pursuing hybrid-electric propulsion.That doesn’t mean it will be a Toyota Prius with wings, but rather it can open some interesting doors for the drone’s design. For example, it could mean the drone will have a combustion engine generating electricity to power electric fans.Alternatively, this could mean it will come with a combustion engine providing propulsion directly, with electrical assistance. Or, indeed, a combination of the two, potentially optimised for different flight conditions.General Atomics’ gambitAt the core of this decision will be efficiency. A hybrid setup could allow the combustion engine to operate closer to its optimum efficiency, potentially reducing fuel consumption significantly.This could offer the drone some important advantages when it comes to stealth capability. For example, it would provide reduced infrared signature under certain operating conditions.It could also offer the drone quieter operation as well as providing greater flexibility in where engines, fans, and exhaust outlets are positioned. In fact, GA is targeting more than 60 hours of unrefueled endurance for NextGen.That’s two and a half days airborne without refuelling. However, that is an engineering target, not an independently demonstrated capability.Another interesting wrinkle is that GA has announced the NextGen will feed on and into its existing Gambit series of modular drones. These are a set of six new drones that can reuse common core components like landing gear, avionics, and other equipment.By sharing hardware, the design and manufacturing process is simplified and made more efficient. By feeding into this architecture, NextGen will not only benefit but can also help lead design for some of the Gambit variants, like its planned flying-wing Gambit 4.In other, but related news, GA has announced that the latest variant of Gambit, called Gambit 6, is beginning to take shape. This will effectively be a ground-attack modification of its existing Gambit 2, AKA the FQ-42A.Gambit 6 to be revealed in 2027According to reports, the company hopes to have a live-firing demonstration of it by early 2027. This drone will operate much in the same way as a conventional manned stealth aircraft with internal munitions bays to reduce radar signature. All of this feeds into the broader idea that the future of air forces will be a combination of manned and unmanned craft working together. Technically known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCAs), both NextGen and Gambit 6 would offer some interesting tactical options in the future.“When we announced the Gambit Series in 2022, we knew that it was an ambitious, multi-stage concept that would require many years before its full power would be realized across all variants,” GA spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said. “It’s not complicated to understand, but it is revolutionary, and revolutions take time,” he added.

title: Why fusion reactors must get hotter than the Sun’s core
content: The Sun sustains nuclear fusion at a core temperature of about 15 million degrees Celsius (27 million °F). Yet scientists developing fusion reactors on Earth often aim for temperatures above 100 million degrees Celsius (180 million °F).If the goal is to harness the process powering our nearest star, why does the fuel needs to become so much hotter?The answer involves more than heat. The Sun’s gravity confines dense plasma, while terrestrial machines must create conditions for useful fusion within a much smaller space. Their fuel and confinement methods also differ.Reaching the Sun’s core temperature alone would therefore fall short of what many reactor designs require.The Sun has gravity on its sideFusion occurs when light atomic nuclei combine, releasing energy. Bringing them together is difficult because nuclei carry positive electrical charges and repel each other. They must approach closely enough for the attractive nuclear force to bind them.Inside the Sun, gravity compresses matter and confines the hot plasma. This provides a dense environment in which nuclei can interact. Magnetic confinement reactors operate with far thinner fuel, giving each nucleus fewer potential partners within a given volume. Raising the temperature increases the likelihood of fusion during those encounters.Temperature describes the particles’ average kinetic energy. As the plasma gets hotter, its nuclei move faster, and a greater proportion of encounters occur at energies favorable for fusion. Quantum tunneling also allows nuclei to penetrate the electrical barrier that would otherwise keep them apart. This process matters in both stars and laboratory fusion.However, higher temperature cannot compensate indefinitely for inadequate density or rapid energy losses. A reactor must establish a workable combination of all three conditions.Reactors use a different fuel recipeThe Sun primarily generates energy through the proton–proton chain, a sequence that ultimately converts hydrogen into helium. Its opening step requires two protons to combine, with one converting into a neutron through the weak nuclear interaction. This reaction proceeds extremely slowly.The Sun’s enormous inventory of particles allows vast numbers of reactions to occur despite that slow individual rate. A terrestrial power plant needs a reaction that can release useful energy within a compact device. Many fusion designs therefore use deuterium and tritium, heavier isotopes of hydrogen.When these nuclei fuse, they produce a helium nucleus and an energetic neutron. Deuterium–tritium fusion is the most readily attainable reaction for terrestrial fusion power, operating at lower temperatures than other leading fuel combinations. Nevertheless, practical designs commonly target temperatures around 100–150 million degrees Celsius (180–270 million °F). ITER’s fusion overview describes a target of approximately 150 million degrees Celsius.Those figures are operating targets, rather than a universal switch-on temperature. Fusion reactions can occur below them; the challenge is achieving a sufficiently high reaction rate while controlling energy losses.Keeping the heat matters as much as creating itScientists assess fusion performance through temperature, particle density, and energy confinement time. Their combination is often called the fusion triple product. As the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics explains, energy confinement time describes how quickly thermal energy escapes from the plasma, rather than how long an experiment runs.Tokamaks and stellarators use magnetic fields to confine plasma. Laser fusion follows another route, compressing and heating a tiny fuel pellet so reactions occur before the fuel disperses. These approaches balance density and confinement time differently. Consequently, saying that Earth simply cannot reproduce stellar pressure gives an incomplete explanation.For sustained operation, fusion must replace enough of the energy the plasma loses. In a burning plasma, fusion reactions themselves supply most of the heating. Achieving ignition means that self-heating can maintain the required temperature without external heating.A temperature record alone therefore cannot demonstrate a practical power source. The fuel must remain sufficiently dense and well insulated for fusion to deliver the required energy. Hotter plasma is one part of that demanding balance.

title: A Natural Compound Found in Everyday Foods Shows Surprising Power Against Lung Cancer
content:
Quercetin is a naturally occurring plant compound found in foods such as onions, citrus fruits, apples, and buckwheat. Known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, this flavonoid has attracted scientific interest for its potential effects on cellular health, immune function, and diseases such as cancer. Credit: Shutterstock
A natural compound found in common foods has shown promising effects against lung cancer cells.
Quercetin, a compound found in citrus fruits, onions, and buckwheat, slowed lung cancer cell division and movement in laboratory experiments. At the highest dose tested, cell migration nearly stopped.
The findings come from researchers at Universitätsklinikum Erlangen at Friedrich-Alexander Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), who examined the compound’s effects in laboratory-grown lung cancer cells, mouse lung tissue sections, and living mice. Their study appeared in
Cell Death Discovery
Lung cancer is the most common cancer worldwide and causes more cancer deaths than any other type. Available treatments do not work for everyone, prompting researchers to investigate additional approaches, including plant compounds such as quercetin, which is known for its anti-inflammatory properties.
Quercetin Targets Several Cancer Cell Processes
The team in the hospital’s Department of Molecular Pneumology found that quercetin affected several processes involved in cancer growth. “Many drugs against lung cancer target a single molecule,” explains Prof. Dr. Susetta Finotto. “Quercetin, by contrast, attacked at several points simultaneously in our experiments.”
Treated tumor cells divided more slowly. In one of the two lung cancer cell types examined, quercetin also lowered oxidative stress. This occurs when reactive oxygen compounds overwhelm cells’ defenses, potentially causing damage that contributes to cancer development.
The effect on movement was particularly striking because migration helps cancer cells spread and establish new tumors, known as metastases. “The higher the quercetin dose, the fewer cancer cells migrated. At the highest dose, the migration almost completely stopped,” reports Christine Carvalho, the study’s lead author.
Quercetin also reduced levels of two proteins, EGFR and PD-L1, in the cancer cells studied. EGFR passes growth signals into cells, while PD-L1 can help tumors evade immune defenses.
Mouse Studies Reveal Immune and Gut Changes
In mouse lung tissue sections, quercetin increased levels of interferon-alpha-2, a signaling molecule that helps the immune system defend against tumors. The researchers also observed changes beyond the lungs, involving the community of microbes living in the gut.
“In the mice that received quercetin, the gut microbiome also changed,” explains Prof. Susetta Finotto. “Bacteria that produce certain short-chain fatty acids were more common.” These fatty acids can enter the bloodstream and reach the lungs, where they can inhibit cancer cell growth.
The mice given quercetin also showed signs of fewer tumor sites. However, only a few animals developed tumors, leaving too little evidence to confirm that finding. Further studies are needed, and whether the effects seen in cells and mice extend to people remains unknown. The experiments also do not establish whether eating quercetin-containing foods would reproduce these results.
“Our results suggest that a quercetin-rich diet could support treatment for lung cancer,” says Prof. Susetta Finotto. “We also think it may have preventive effects. We want to investigate that next.”
Reference: “Immunoregulatory role of quercetin in lung cancer” by Christine Carvalho, Elvedina Nendel, Susanne Mittler, Sonja Trump, Adriana Geiger, Jonas Willar, Mircea T. Chiriac, Stefan Wirtz, Carol I. Geppert and Susetta Finotto, 14 September 2026,
Cell Death Discovery

title: A Last Refuge: Australian Waters Could Save a Critically Endangered Ocean Predator
content:
The green sawfish is a critically endangered species of ray known for its sharklike body and long, flattened snout lined with sharp teeth. Once widespread across tropical coastal waters, its populations have declined dramatically due to overfishing, accidental capture in fishing gear, and habitat loss. Credit: Shutterstock
Despite decades of research, major gaps in scientists’ understanding of green sawfish could complicate efforts to save the species.
Green sawfish have disappeared from large parts of their former range, but northern Australia still supports some of the last relatively intact populations of this critically endangered species. A new scientific review suggests these waters could be central to the animal’s survival, although major gaps in researchers’ knowledge continue to complicate conservation efforts.
Green sawfish are a type of ray with a sharklike body and a distinctive, tooth-lined snout resembling a saw. Overfishing and habitat loss have driven their decline worldwide. Researchers at Murdoch University’s Centre for Sustainable Aquatic Ecosystems, part of the Harry Butler Institute, have now brought together decades of scientific findings to identify the species’ remaining strongholds and determine where further research is needed.
Northern Australia Offers a Rare Refuge
“Although the species has disappeared from large parts of its historic range, including parts of Africa and southern Asia, northern Australia still supports some of the last intact populations left anywhere on Earth,” said Dr. Jack Ingelbrecht, a postdoctoral research associate who led the review alongside Associate Professor David Morgan. Ingelbrecht added, “We’re fortunate that the main factors responsible for the global decline of sawfish are less severe in northern Australia.”
Western Australia’s Pilbara region is particularly valuable because it contains important green sawfish habitat and populations that remain relatively healthy. “The Pilbara region in particular has become one of the world’s most important areas for green sawfish research, as it still supports relatively healthy populations of this species and provides critical habitat,” said Morgan, who has studied Australian sawfish for more than 25 years. “It gives us a rare opportunity to understand how green sawfish use their environment, and identify which conservation measures would best facilitate their recovery.”
Why Australia Leads Green Sawfish Research
The survival of green sawfish in Australian waters has also shaped the global scientific understanding of the species. “To research something, you first need specimens to study. Naturally, opportunities for green sawfish research will be greater in areas where this species still occurs in relatively high numbers,” Ingelbrecht explained.
Green Sawfish. Credit: David Morgan/Murdoch University
“Our review found that, for decades, Australia has been the global leader in green sawfish research. This is partly because green sawfish populations have been wiped out in many countries, but still exist in Australia,” he said. Australia’s contribution extends across many different areas of scientific investigation. “Interestingly, when we looked at the specific types of information that have been produced, we found that Australia has also been at the forefront of almost every major sub-discipline of research relating to green sawfish.”
The research team compiled existing studies into a single resource intended to support conservation planning and future investigations. “Renowned zoologist Ferdinando Boero said it best: ‘you can’t protect what you don’t know,'” Ingelbrecht said. “It’s incredibly difficult to stay up to date with research on any topic, particularly when there’s a lot of information to cover. Ultimately, if conservation experts don’t fully understand the species they’re trying to protect, they can’t implement the most-suitable recovery initiatives.”
Critical Questions Remain Unanswered
Despite Australia’s extensive research history, the review identified substantial gaps in the information needed to protect green sawfish. “By synthesizing the current knowledge of green sawfish, we wanted to provide an all-in-one resource to guide conservation efforts and researchers, alike,” Ingelbrecht said.
The most pressing uncertainties concern how many green sawfish survive, where their most important habitats are located, and how many individuals are old enough to reproduce. “Sadly, when it comes to the research areas most relevant to conservation – the size of remaining populations, the locations of critical habitat, and the number of mature individuals present in the wild – we realized that there’s very little information currently available.”
These missing data make it difficult to design conservation strategies suited to the species’ biological needs. “Research is the lifeblood of conservation. In order to be successful, recovery efforts often need to be tailored towards the species they’re intended for. To do that, you need scientific input,” Ingelbrecht said.
The Race to Prevent Extinction
As green sawfish disappear from more of their historical range, Australia’s role in protecting the species could become increasingly significant. “Conservation biologists bear the responsibility of enhancing recovery initiatives through research. If green sawfish populations continue to decline, that responsibility – that burden – will fall more and more towards Australia,” Ingelbrecht warned.
The researchers nevertheless believe extinction can still be prevented if scientific research and conservation measures receive sufficient support. “It’s not over yet. There’s still a genuine opportunity to turn things around. With the right support, the right research, and the right conservation measures, we can ensure the survival of green sawfish. I hope Australia sets an example the rest of the world can follow,” Ingelbrecht said.
Reference: “The Critically Endangered green sawfish (Pristis zijsron): current knowledge and future directions” by Jack Ingelbrecht, Barbara E. Wueringer, Tyler N. Dornan, Penelope T. Dantas, Travis Fazeldean and David L. Morgan, 11 September 2026,
Reviews in Fish Biology and Fisheries
DOI: 10.1007/s11160-026-10088-7

title: Do Spiders Dream? Scientists Discover a Mysterious Sleep State
content:
The spider Portia fimbriata in a sleeping position, hanging upside down beneath its self-spun web. Credit: Daniela C. Rößler
Scientists have discovered that spiders experience REM-like sleep, complete with twitching muscles and moving eyes, raising the intriguing possibility that they might dream.
Spiders may have more in common with sleeping humans than scientists previously realized. Researchers at the University of Bonn have discovered that Australian jumping spiders experience two distinct stages of sleep, including a state that closely resembles REM sleep in humans. During this stage, the spiders move their eyes and twitch their muscles, behaviors that raise intriguing questions about the origins of sleep and whether spiders might experience something resembling dreams.
The findings provide the first comprehensive experimental confirmation of regulated sleep in spiders. They also suggest that complex sleep patterns may be far more widespread throughout the animal kingdom than previously understood.
In humans and other vertebrates, sleep involves multiple stages, including REM (rapid eye movement) sleep. This stage is associated with rapid eye movements, changes in muscle activity, and vivid dreaming in humans. Scientists have long wondered whether animals with very different nervous systems, including spiders, experience comparable sleep states.
To investigate, researchers from the Institute of Organismic Biology at the University of Bonn turned to an unusual subject: the Australian jumping spider
Portia fimbriata
The spider Portia fimbriata hunting an orb-web spider. Credit: Daniela C. Rößler
A Remarkably Intelligent Spider
The spider belongs to the genus Portia, a group of predators known for their sophisticated hunting techniques. Unlike many spiders that primarily capture insects, Portia species specialize in hunting other spiders.
One of their most remarkable strategies involves manipulating the webs of their prey. By producing vibrations that imitate insects struggling in silk, these spiders can lure web-building spiders toward them. Such complex hunting behavior suggests an unusual capacity for learning and adapting to different situations.
Despite their impressive abilities, these predators are quite small. A fully grown
Portia fimbriata
is roughly the size of a one-euro coin.
Their sophisticated behavior made them particularly interesting subjects for investigating sleep. Scientists wanted to determine whether these spiders simply become inactive at night or enter a genuine, biologically regulated sleep state similar to those observed in vertebrates.
Scientists Discover Two Distinct Sleep Stages
The researchers found convincing behavioral evidence that
Portia fimbriata
does more than rest. The spiders exhibit regulated sleep with two clearly distinguishable stages.
One of these stages closely resembles REM sleep, a well-known phase of human sleep characterized by rapid eye movements and muscle twitches.
During the spiders’ REM-like periods, the researchers observed eye movements and twitching muscles, suggesting that certain features of sleep may be shared by animals whose nervous systems are dramatically different from our own.
The discovery is especially significant because most scientific knowledge about sleep has come from studies of vertebrates, including humans, other mammals, birds, and reptiles. Until now, comprehensive experimental evidence establishing true sleep behavior in spiders had been lacking.
Although the REM-like movements are intriguing, they do not demonstrate that spiders dream. Determining whether spiders experience anything comparable to human dreams would require evidence beyond the behavioral observations available in this study.
How Researchers Studied Sleeping Spiders
To examine the spiders’ nighttime behavior, the scientists monitored individual
Portia fimbriata
specimens over multiple days and nights.
Each spider was kept in a small plastic dish measuring 12 centimeters in diameter. The researchers exposed the animals to different lighting conditions to investigate their daily activity cycles and determine how their behavior changed between day and night.
High-resolution video recordings allowed the team to examine the spiders’ movements in detail. During nighttime observations, infrared cameras captured their sleeping positions, periods of inactivity, and episodes of REM-like behavior without requiring visible light.
But remaining motionless is not necessarily proof of sleep. Animals can become inactive for several reasons, so the researchers needed additional evidence to distinguish actual sleep from ordinary rest.
They tested the spiders’ responses to sound and measured how quickly the animals reacted. These experiments helped determine whether the spiders became less responsive to external disturbances during their resting periods, an important characteristic of sleep.
The team also investigated a phenomenon known as “sleep rebound,” which occurs when an animal compensates for interrupted or insufficient sleep by sleeping more afterward. Testing for this response helped establish whether the spiders’ rest was regulated by an underlying biological need.
Together, these observations and experiments provided evidence that the spiders experience genuine sleep rather than simply remaining inactive.
The Challenge of Identifying Sleep in Spiders
Studying sleep in spiders presents difficulties that researchers do not typically encounter when investigating humans or other mammals.
One major obstacle was identifying a stimulus that would reliably awaken the spiders during experiments. Spiders perceive their surroundings very differently from humans, making it challenging to design tests that could consistently measure their responses.
The researchers also had to be careful when interpreting the unusual movements recorded during the REM-like stage. Although eye movements and muscle twitches resemble behaviors associated with REM sleep in vertebrates, similar outward movements do not necessarily indicate identical processes inside the nervous system.
Another important limitation was the inability to directly measure the spiders’ brain activity. Instead, the researchers had to base their conclusions entirely on observable behavior.
To overcome these challenges, they collected extensive high-resolution video recordings over long observation periods. This provided the detail needed to examine subtle movements and sleep patterns, but it also generated enormous amounts of data that had to be analyzed.
What Spider Sleep Reveals About Evolution
The discovery could have important implications for understanding how sleep evolved.
REM sleep is one of the most fascinating and still incompletely understood aspects of human biology. Although it is closely associated with dreaming in humans, scientists continue to investigate its broader functions and evolutionary history.
Finding REM-like behavior in spiders raises the possibility that some features of complex sleep are shared across a much wider range of animals than previously established.
Spiders and vertebrates have very different nervous systems, yet both appear capable of entering distinct behavioral sleep states. Understanding these similarities could help researchers identify fundamental properties of sleep that have persisted through evolution or developed independently in different animal groups.
The findings also open new opportunities in behavioral biology, neuroscience, and chronobiology, the study of biological rhythms and internal clocks. They may be particularly valuable for understanding how sleep functions in animals with relatively simple nervous systems.
Rather than limiting sleep research to humans and traditional laboratory animals, the scientists recommend studying a much broader diversity of species, especially those with unusual nervous systems or highly specialized adaptations.
Such comparisons could help reveal whether sleep serves a universal biological purpose and whether some of its essential features originated very early in animal evolution.
Despite decades of research, many basic questions about why animals sleep and what happens during different sleep stages remain unanswered, even in humans.
Could Spiders Dream? Scientists Want to Find Out
The University of Bonn researchers are now extending their investigations to other spider species to better understand how sleep and REM-like states evolved across this diverse group of animals.
They also plan to compare spiders sleeping in laboratory environments with those living in the wild. These studies could reveal whether natural surroundings influence sleep patterns in ways that controlled laboratory conditions cannot fully capture.
Another major research direction involves exploring the relationship between sleep and intelligence. Because Portia spiders display sophisticated hunting and learning abilities, they provide an interesting opportunity to investigate whether sleep contributes to cognitive processes in animals with very different brains from humans.
Future studies will also examine what happens inside the nervous systems of spiders and insects during sleep. Direct measurements of neural activity could help determine whether the REM-like behaviors observed in spiders involve processes comparable to those found in vertebrates.
The researchers are additionally interested in how environmental changes influence sleep. In particular, they hope to investigate the effects of climate change and human activities, including artificial light at night (ALAN), on the sleep behavior of spiders and other small animals.
Artificial nighttime lighting can alter the natural cycle of light and darkness that many organisms use to regulate their daily rhythms. Understanding how spiders respond to these disruptions could provide new insights into the broader ecological consequences of human activity.
For now, the findings establish something remarkable: even a tiny jumping spider can experience distinct, regulated stages of sleep, including one that resembles REM sleep in humans.
Whether those sleeping spiders actually dream remains an open question, but their unusual nighttime behavior offers scientists a new way to investigate one of biology’s oldest mysteries.
Reference: “Behavioral evidence for two-stage sleep in spiders” by Nadja Geiger, Maxim Q. Capelle, Phillip Rosentreter, Marie E. Herberstein, Armin Bahl, Massimo De Agrò, Barrett A. Klein and Daniela C. Rößler, 26 October 2026,
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2618030123

title: Scientists Uncover Why Breast Cancer Becomes Deadlier As We Age
content:
Breast cancer risk increases with age, with most cases diagnosed in women over 50. As the body ages, changes in immune function, hormone levels, and chronic inflammation can influence how breast cancer develops and progresses. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists have uncovered a biological mechanism that may help explain why breast cancer becomes more dangerous with age.
In older mice, breast cancer was far more likely to spread to the lungs, even when the original tumors grew at roughly the same rate as those in younger animals. Researchers at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center have identified an inflammation-related receptor that appears to play a central role in this age-related increase in metastasis.
The researchers found that genetically removing the receptor, known as RAGE, almost completely eliminated the increased spread of cancer in older mice. Published May 15, 2026, in
Communications Biology
, the findings suggest that changes occurring throughout the body during aging can influence how aggressively cancer behaves.
How Aging Creates Conditions That Help Cancer Spread
The study focused on RAGE (Receptor for Advanced Glycation End-products), a receptor on the surface of cells that amplifies inflammatory signals. Aging increased levels of molecules that activate RAGE, including the proteins S100 and HMGB1. These molecules were found in both primary tumors and metastatic sites, where the resulting inflammatory activity helped cancer cells invade surrounding tissues and spread.
“Our study addresses a major gap by showing that aging dramatically increases breast cancer metastasis and that this effect depends on RAGE, a receptor on the surface of cells that fuels inflammation,” says Barry Hudson, PhD, associate professor of oncology at Georgetown Lombardi and corresponding author for this article. “Most laboratory studies rely on young mice, which has limited our understanding of how aging itself alters the host environment, including immune function and chronic inflammatory states that, in turn, influence cancer behavior.”
“These findings show that aging doesn’t just increase cancer risk — it actively changes the body in ways that help tumors spread,” says Hudson. “RAGE appears to be a key mediator of these harmful age-related pathways.”
An Unexpected Opportunity to Study Cancer in Older Animals
The research benefited from an unusual circumstance during the COVID-19 pandemic. Reduced laboratory activity meant some mouse colonies were allowed to age longer than originally planned. Because maintaining older laboratory mice is expensive and time-consuming, the situation gave researchers a rare opportunity to examine how aging affects cancer progression. They compared younger and older animals across three mouse models of triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive form of the disease.
The team also investigated whether the findings had parallels in humans. An analysis of breast cancer data from more than 1,000 patients showed that higher expression of AGER (the gene encoding RAGE), along with elevated activity in related inflammatory genes, was associated with poorer outcomes. Although these associations do not establish that RAGE causes metastasis in patients, they support the potential clinical relevance of the animal experiments.
A Potential Treatment Target Already Under Investigation
RAGE is being studied as a therapeutic target in several diseases associated with aging. Earlier research from the Georgetown team showed that the RAGE inhibitor TTP488 (azeliragon) could suppress breast cancer metastasis in preclinical models. In the latest experiments, the drug also reduced the invasiveness of cancer cells exposed to blood serum from aged mice, which otherwise promoted more invasive behavior.
A clinical study at Georgetown Lombardi is now evaluating TTP488 in breast cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, with particular attention to safety and cognitive outcomes. The drug has previously demonstrated a favorable safety profile in humans, although its ability to prevent breast cancer metastasis in patients remains unproven.
“This study highlights the importance of the host environment in cancer. While cancer is often viewed as driven primarily by mutations intrinsic to tumor cells, systemic factors such as aging and inflammation play a critical role in shaping how cancers behave,” says Hudson. “Most deaths due to cancer occur because tumors spread to other organs, so understanding these influences may help identify new strategies to limit metastasis.”
Reference: “Aging promotes a RAGE-dependent increase in breast cancer metastasis” by Philip Miller, Sunita Chopra, Melinda Magna, Jiaxiang Tao, Carlos Benitez, Thomas Heist, Nanette H. Bishopric, Jeanne S. Mandelblatt, Julia Panov, Joyce M. Slingerland and Barry I. Hudson, 15 May 2026,
Communications Biology

title: Scientists Discover a Surprising New Target for Treating Type 2 Diabetes
content:
Type 2 diabetes is a chronic metabolic disease in which the body becomes resistant to insulin or fails to produce enough insulin to maintain normal blood sugar levels. Over time, elevated blood sugar can damage blood vessels, nerves, and organs, increasing the risk of heart disease, kidney disease, and vision loss. Credit: Stock
A clinical trial has uncovered a molecular change in skeletal muscle that may help explain why exercise improves insulin sensitivity in people with Type 2 diabetes.
A protein found in unusually high amounts in the muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes may be interfering with the body’s ability to respond to insulin. Researchers discovered that removing the protein, known as Miro1, restored insulin responsiveness in preclinical models, suggesting a possible new approach to treating insulin resistance.
The study, published in
Nature Communications
, also found that aerobic exercise reduced Miro1 levels in people with Type 2 diabetes. Those reductions occurred alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity and the muscles’ ability to produce energy.
Miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase1) sits on the outer membrane of mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of a cell’s usable energy. Skeletal muscle plays a major role in regulating blood sugar because it absorbs glucose from the bloodstream in response to insulin. When muscle becomes resistant to insulin, glucose is less effectively removed from the blood, contributing to the elevated blood sugar associated with Type 2 diabetes.
To investigate Miro1’s involvement, scientists examined its effects in cells, preclinical models, and people with Type 2 diabetes. Their experiments showed that excess Miro1 impaired insulin responses in muscle, while removing the protein reversed those effects in preclinical models.
“Insulin resistance in muscle is at the heart of Type 2 diabetes, and its molecular causes have remained frustratingly unclear. This study, the product of years of work, identifies Miro1 as a key part of the answer. By tracing Miro1 from cells to preclinical models to patients, we show that Miro1 accumulation impairs the muscle’s response to insulin, that removing it causally restores that response in our models, and that exercise reverses its buildup in people. For the field, this is a new therapeutic target. For patients, it deepens our understanding of why exercise is so effective and opens a path toward treatments that could one day complement it,” said senior author Dr. John P. Kirwan.
The researchers also conducted a randomized controlled trial involving participants with obesity and Type 2 diabetes. One group performed aerobic exercise, while another received standard medical care. Participants assigned to exercise showed lower Miro1 levels in their muscles, together with improved insulin sensitivity and mitochondrial energy production.
These human findings support a connection between exercise, Miro1, and metabolic health. However, they do not establish that reducing Miro1 is responsible for the benefits of exercise. The preclinical experiments provide more direct evidence that the protein can influence insulin responses.
Graphical summary of the role of Miro1 in skeletal muscle. Credit: Kirwan Lab
Kirwan led the research while working at LSU’s Pennington Biomedical Research Center. He has since been appointed executive director of the OU Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma, where he will continue investigating the biological mechanisms of diabetes and potential treatments.
The study’s first author, Elizabeth Heintz, conducted research as a doctoral candidate in Pennington Biomedical’s Integrated Physiology and Molecular Medicine Laboratory. Co-corresponding author Christopher Axelrod has since joined Kirwan at the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center.
“This research exemplifies the breadth of scientific discovery at Pennington Biomedical, where research spans all levels, from basic science that reveals the biological mechanisms underlying disease to clinical studies and population-based research that informs public health,” said Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical. “Dr. Kirwan and his team’s findings on Miro1 demonstrate the value of this integrated approach, connecting fundamental discoveries about muscle function with insights into insulin resistance and the benefits of exercise in people with Type 2 diabetes. This work is advancing our understanding of diabetes and helping lay the foundation for future approaches to prevention and treatment.”
Although removing Miro1 improved insulin responses in experimental models, researchers have not yet established whether targeting the protein would be safe or effective as a treatment for people. Further studies will need to clarify how Miro1 contributes to insulin resistance and whether modifying its activity can improve blood sugar regulation.
At the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center, Kirwan plans to build on these findings through research that connects laboratory discoveries with studies involving people with diabetes.
“Type 2 diabetes is an affliction in Oklahoma and nationally,” he said. “Ultimately, we are looking for cures, and we hope these recent findings could be part of the solution.”
Reference: “Miro1 mediates skeletal muscle insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes” by Elizabeth C. Heintz, Wagner S. Dantas, Analisa L. Taylor, Elizabeth R. M. Zunica, Kathryn P. Belmont, Jackson M. Slone, Jacob T. Mey, Robbie Beyl, Bolormaa Vandanmagsar, Hailey A. Parry, Peter Ajayi, Brian Glancy, Christopher L. Axelrod and John P. Kirwan, 19 October 2026,
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77278-6
The research was supported by the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the National Institute on Aging, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

title: Eating a Handful of Peanuts Could Change Your Blood in a Surprising Way, Study Finds
content:
Peanuts are nutrient-rich legumes packed with protein, healthy unsaturated fats, fiber, vitamins, and minerals. Although commonly considered nuts, they grow underground and belong to the same plant family as beans and lentils. Credit: Shutterstock
A handful of peanuts may leave a telltale signature in your blood, and researchers have linked that pattern to a lower risk of type 2 diabetes.
What happens inside your body after eating a handful of peanuts? Beyond providing protein, fiber, and healthy fats, these popular legumes appear to leave a distinctive chemical fingerprint in the bloodstream. Scientists have now linked this pattern of circulating fats to a lower risk of type 2 diabetes, offering new clues about the complex relationship between diet, body weight, and metabolic health.
To investigate, researchers combined a six-month dietary experiment with data from a long-term population study involving more than 27,000 people. Their findings revealed how peanut consumption reshapes certain blood lipids and suggested that body mass index plays an important role in the observed connection to diabetes risk.
Looking Beyond Cholesterol
Cholesterol tests capture only part of the fat circulating in the bloodstream. A technique called lipidomics provides a more detailed inventory, revealing differences among lipid classes that conventional measurements may miss.
The type of fat you eat helps shape how your body processes and stores it. Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats can improve blood lipid profiles and reduce inflammation, helping address the cardiometabolic risks associated with unhealthy diets.
Even saturated fatty acids are not a uniform group. Very long chain saturated fatty acids (VLCSFA), which contain more than 20 carbon atoms, may have distinctive metabolic effects. Peanuts, which are legumes, supply these fats alongside monounsaturated fatty acids.
Tracking the Effects of Peanuts
Dr. Inés Domínguez-López and Professor Matthias Schulze at the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbruecke worked with University of Barcelona researchers to investigate how peanuts influence this broader lipid landscape.
They began with ARISTOTLE, a randomized controlled trial involving 63 healthy adults ages 18 to 33. For six months, participants consumed either 25 grams (0.88 ounces) of skin-roasted peanuts, 32 grams (1.13 ounces) of peanut butter, or 32 grams (1.13 ounces) of a control butter containing peanut oil each day.
Using high-resolution mass spectrometry, an approach known as “deep lipidomics,” the team identified a characteristic pattern of blood fats following peanut consumption. They called it the “Peanut Lipidomic Signature” (PeLS).
A Different Mix of Blood Fats
Peanut consumption significantly increased certain very long-chain saturated fatty acids, particularly C24:0 and C22:0. These were preferentially incorporated into specific lipid classes, including ceramides, through processes involving enzymes that lengthen fatty acid chains.
“This is not merely a simple increase in fat levels but a complex ‘remodeling’ of the lipidome,” explains first author Domínguez-López.
“By characterizing this specific peanut lipid signature, we have uncovered a potential biological marker that links dietary fat quality to metabolic outcomes,” explains Schulze.
The researchers then examined samples and records from EPIC-Potsdam, a long-term population study with more than 27,000 participants. Its data included people who developed type 2 diabetes (774 cases) and cardiovascular disease (545 cases).
Where Body Weight Fits In
The peanut lipid signature was associated with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes, but not cardiovascular disease. Much of the relationship with diabetes was statistically explained by body mass index (BMI).
“This suggests that the positive metabolic effects of these specific peanut-derived lipids may be linked to their ability to support a healthier body weight or stabilize metabolic processes related to adiposity,” Domínguez-López says.
Affordable and widely available, peanuts could be a practical addition to a balanced diet that supports metabolic health, with their distinctive blood lipid signature linked to a lower risk of type 2 diabetes.
Reference: “Peanuts-derived plasma lipids and lower risk of type 2 diabetes: association mediated by body mass index—an intervention and case-cohort study” by Inés Domínguez-López, Fabian Eichelmann, Isabella Parilli-Moser, Sara Hurtado-Barroso, Rosa M Lamuela-Raventós and Matthias B Schulze, 17 September 2026,
The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
DOI: 10.1016/j.ajcnut.2026.101527

title: Scientists Use Light To Build a New Generation of Drug Molecules
content:
Chemistry
Artistic illustration of a light-driven reaction for constructing three-dimensional BCH molecular structures. Credit: Emily R.-C. Yang
The flat molecular structures commonly found in medicines can limit their properties.
A new light-powered chemical technique could give scientists more freedom to design drug molecules with complex three-dimensional shapes. Researchers at the
University of Hong Kong (HKU)
have developed a way to produce molecular structures that could serve as alternatives to benzene rings, which are widely used in medicines but can sometimes limit their properties.
Led by Professor Jian He from HKU’s Department of Chemistry, the team developed specialized copper(I) photosensitizers that use visible light to construct bicyclo[2.1.1]hexanes, or BCHs. Published in
Nature Chemistry
, the research addresses two major challenges in producing these structures: the limited range of compatible starting materials and unwanted chemical reactions that interfere with synthesis.
Why Drug Designers Are Looking Beyond Benzene
Benzene rings are common in pharmaceutical compounds because their chemical stability makes them reliable frameworks for arranging other molecular components. However, their flat shape and relatively lipophilic nature can contribute to poor water solubility or unfavorable interactions with biological targets, potentially limiting the performance of certain drug candidates.
BCHs offer a compact, three-dimensional alternative that can fulfill a similar structural role while giving molecules a different shape. Incorporating these structures could allow medicinal chemists to adjust properties such as solubility, selectivity, and metabolic stability. However, producing a broad variety of BCH compounds has remained difficult using existing synthetic techniques.
Catalytic photosensitisation strategies for the synthesis of BCH bioisosteres via intermolecular cycloadditions. Image adapted from Tang et al., Nature Chemistry (2026). Credit: The University of Hong Kong
Using Visible Light to Build More Complex Molecules
One way to make BCHs is to combine bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes, known as BCBs, with alkenes. BCBs contain highly strained molecular rings that can be transformed into more complex structures. Unfortunately, conventional reactions often work with only certain starting materials and can suffer from unstable catalysts or unwanted polymerization, which causes molecules to join into chains rather than form the desired products.
To overcome these limitations, the HKU researchers developed a new class of copper(I) photosensitizers. When exposed to visible light, these compounds absorb energy and transfer it to a starting material, helping drive the formation of BCH structures. By adjusting the energy properties of the copper complexes, the team reduced competing reactions and expanded the types of molecules that could participate.
The researchers also demonstrated control over the placement of chemical groups on the BCH framework. They successfully produced BCH compounds on a gram scale and modified the resulting structures with additional functional groups, demonstrating the method’s versatility for future medicinal chemistry research.
Professor He explained, “The heteroleptic copper(I) photosensitizers developed by our team provide a new approach to the efficient and selective synthesis of BCHs. By modulating the triplet energy levels of copper complexes, we have effectively suppressed polymerization side reactions and expanded the substrate scope to include electron-deficient alkenes, enynes, dienes, and even aliphatic alkenes. This opens new opportunities for sustainable chemical production and the development of more diverse drug candidates.”
